Doubling the Kelvin temperature multiplies the volume by 2, and halving the pressure multiplies it by a further factor of 2, giving 2 × 2 = 4 times the original volume. Hence (d), four times (printed as Four time). Answering double takes account of the temperature change only, and reduced to half would require the opposite changes.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Remains same  (b) Double  (c) Reduced to half  (d) Four time

questions.question: The molar volume of oxygen gas is 22.4 dm³ at:
questions.answer: (a) 0°C and 1 atm
questions.explanation: 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹ is the molar volume of any ideal gas at standard temperature and pressure, that is at 0°C (273 K) and 1 atm. At 25°C and 0.5 atm the molar volume would be 0.0821 × 298/0.5 = 48.9 dm³ mol⁻¹, and 0 K is unattainable and would in any case give zero volume. Hence (a).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) 0°C and 1 atm  (b) 25°C and 0.5 atm  (c) 0 K and 1 atm  (d) 25 K and 0.5 atm

questions.question: Under similar condition CH₄ gas diffuses........ times faster than SO₂ gas:
questions.answer: (c) 4 times
questions.explanation: The book's printed answer key gives (c) 4 times, and that printed key is followed here. There is, however, a clear discrepancy: a strict Graham's-law calculation gives r(CH₄)/r(SO₂) = √(M(SO₂)/M(CH₄)) = √(64/16) = √4 = 2, that is 2 times, which is option (b). The value 4 is obtained if the molar masses themselves are divided (64/16) instead of their square roots, and 16 comes from using the ratio of masses squared; 1.5 has no basis for this pair. Students should note that by correct calculation the answer is (b) 2 times, while the book's printed key states (c) 4 times; option (c) is retained only to match the printed key.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) 1.5 time  (b) 2 times  (c) 4 times  (d) 16 times

questions.question:
State the following gas laws.
(i) Avogadro's law
(ii) Charles law
questions.answer:
(i) Avogadro's law: Equal volumes of all gases, measured at the same temperature and pressure, contain an equal number of molecules (equal number of moles). Mathematically, at constant temperature and pressure, V ∝ n, so V/n = constant and V₁/n₁ = V₂/n₂. One mole of any gas at STP occupies 22.4 dm³ and contains 6.02 × 10²³ molecules.
(ii) Charles law: At constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute (Kelvin) temperature, V ∝ T at constant P and n, so V/T = constant and V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂. Since the volume at 0°C is V₀, the volume at t°C is V = V₀(1 + t/273); a graph of V against T (in kelvin) is a straight line through the origin, and the graph of V against t meets the temperature axis at −273°C.
questions.explanation: Avogadro's law connects the amount of gas with its volume and leads to the molar volume of 22.4 dm³ at STP; Charles's law connects volume with absolute temperature at constant pressure. In both laws the temperature must be expressed in kelvin, because only then is volume directly proportional to temperature. Charles's law holds for an ideal gas and breaks down at low temperature, where a real gas liquefies; its extrapolated zero volume nevertheless defines absolute zero.

questions.question: State main postulates of kinetic molecular theory of gas.
questions.answer:
The main postulates of the kinetic molecular theory of gases are:
(i) A gas consists of a very large number of tiny particles (molecules or atoms) moving randomly in all directions at high speed.
(ii) The actual volume of the molecules is negligible compared with the total volume of the container, so most of the space in a gas is empty.
(iii) There are no appreciable attractive or repulsive forces between the molecules except during a collision, so the molecules move independently of one another.
(iv) Collisions of the molecules with one another and with the walls of the container are perfectly elastic, so no kinetic energy is lost.
(v) The molecules travel in straight lines between collisions, and the pressure of the gas is produced by their collisions with the walls of the container.
(vi) The average kinetic energy of the molecules is directly proportional to the absolute temperature (KE per molecule = 3/2 kT and per mole = 3/2 RT) and is the same for all gases at the same temperature.
(vii) The effect of gravity on the molecular motion is negligible.
questions.explanation: These postulates form an idealised model: molecular volume and intermolecular forces are deliberately ignored so that the simple relation PV = nRT can be derived from them. Real gases approach this model at high temperature and low pressure and depart from it when the molecules are close and slow. The postulate that average kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature is the link between the macroscopic temperature and molecular motion, and it explains why equal volumes of different gases at the same temperature have the same molar kinetic energy.

questions.question:
Explain the following.
(i) Pressure and its various units
(ii) Absolute zero
questions.answer:
(i) Pressure: Pressure is the force exerted normally per unit area, P = F/A. In a gas it is produced by the continuous collisions of the molecules with the walls of the container. The SI unit is the pascal (Pa = N m⁻²). Other units are the atmosphere (atm), the torr, the millimetre of mercury (mm Hg), the bar, the pound per square inch (psi) and the dyne cm⁻². Conversions: 1 atm = 760 mm Hg = 760 torr = 101,325 Pa = 101.325 kPa = 1.01325 bar = 14.7 psi = 1.013 × 10⁶ dyne cm⁻²; 1 torr = 1 mm Hg.
(ii) Absolute zero: Absolute zero is the temperature at which the volume (and the pressure) of an ideal gas would theoretically become zero, that is −273.15°C. It is the zero of the Kelvin scale (0 K), so K = °C + 273. At absolute zero the translational kinetic energy of the molecules would be minimum. It is a limiting temperature that cannot be reached in practice, although temperatures within a small fraction of a kelvin above it have been produced in laboratories.
questions.explanation: Pressure is measured with a barometer when it is atmospheric pressure and with a manometer when it is the pressure of an enclosed gas; the height of the mercury column is the origin of the units mm Hg and torr. Since 1 atm = 760 torr = 101.325 kPa, any of these units can be converted into another. Absolute zero is the lower limit of the Kelvin scale; gas-law calculations must measure temperature from it, which is why Celsius values are converted by adding 273.

questions.question: What is liquid air? Mention its three uses.
questions.answer:
Liquid air: When ordinary air is compressed and cooled to a very low temperature (about −196°C to −200°C) it condenses to a pale bluish liquid called liquid air. It is a mixture of liquid nitrogen (b.p. −196°C), liquid oxygen (b.p. −183°C) and liquid argon, and its components are separated by fractional distillation.
Three uses:
(i) As a coolant: liquid air is used as a refrigerant for the rapid freezing and preservation of food, blood, tissues and vaccines, and for producing very low temperatures in laboratories.
(ii) As a source of oxygen: the oxygen obtained from liquid air is used in hospitals, in oxy-acetylene welding and cutting, in steel making and as an oxidant in rocket fuel.
(iii) As a source of nitrogen and rare gases: nitrogen from liquid air is used in the manufacture of ammonia and fertilizers and as an inert atmosphere in industry, while argon, neon and other rare gases are used in lamps and discharge tubes.
questions.explanation: Liquid air is a physical mixture and not a compound, so its components keep their own boiling points and can be separated by fractional distillation. Its very low temperature is the basis of its use as a coolant, while the oxygen and nitrogen it supplies make it an important industrial raw material. Because liquid oxygen strongly supports combustion, liquid air must be handled carefully and kept away from organic materials.

questions.question: What is plasma? Give its significance in daily life.
questions.answer:
Plasma: Plasma is the fourth state of matter. It is an ionized gas, a mixture of positive ions, free electrons and un-ionized atoms and molecules, produced when a gas is heated to a very high temperature or subjected to a strong electric field so that its atoms lose electrons. It is electrically conducting and is affected by electric and magnetic fields. Examples are the matter of the sun and stars, lightning, the glowing gas in fluorescent tubes and neon signs, and the flame of an electric arc.
Significance in daily life:
(i) Fluorescent tube lights, neon signs and plasma display screens glow because of plasma.
(ii) Lightning and the aurora are natural plasma phenomena, and plasma arcs are used in welding and cutting metals and in energy-saving lamps.
(iii) Plasma technology is used for sterilizing medical equipment and for etching and coating in the electronics industry, and controlled nuclear fusion, a future energy source, depends on plasma.
questions.explanation: Plasma differs from an ordinary gas because a significant fraction of its atoms are ionized, so it contains free charges and conducts electricity. It is the most abundant state of matter in the universe, since stars are made of plasma, although on Earth it occurs naturally only in lightning and the upper atmosphere. Its practical importance comes from its ability to conduct current, emit light and carry very high energy, which is used in lighting, displays, welding, sterilization and fusion research.

questions.question: State and explain Dalton's law of partial pressure. Give practical applications of Dalton's law.
questions.answer:
Statement: Dalton's law of partial pressure states that the total pressure exerted by a mixture of two or more non-reacting gases in a fixed volume at a given temperature is equal to the sum of the partial pressures of the individual gases. P(total) = P₁ + P₂ + P₃ + ...
Explanation: The partial pressure of a gas in a mixture is the pressure that gas would exert if it alone occupied the same volume at the same temperature. In a mixture the molecules of each gas fill the whole container and strike the walls independently of the molecules of the other gases, since the gases do not react and the volume available to each is the same. Each gas therefore contributes its own pressure and the contributions simply add. For ideal gases Pᵢ = nᵢRT/V, so P(total) = (n₁ + n₂ + ...)RT/V = n(total)RT/V, and the partial pressure of a component is Pᵢ = xᵢP(total), where xᵢ is its mole fraction.
Practical applications:
(i) Collection of a gas over water: the pressure of the wet gas is the sum of the pressure of the gas and the vapour pressure of water, so P(gas) = P(total) − P(H₂O vapour).
(ii) Respiration: in the lungs, oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out, and this exchange depends on the partial pressures of the gases in the alveolar air and in the blood, not on the total pressure.
(iii) Diving and mountaineering: the physiological effect of each component of air (O₂, N₂, CO₂) depends on its partial pressure, which is why gas mixtures for divers are adjusted with depth.
(iv) In hospitals the composition of oxygen and of anaesthetic gas mixtures is controlled by partial pressures; the law is also used in the preparation and analysis of gas mixtures and in the storage and transport of gases.
questions.explanation: The law follows directly from the kinetic model: in a mixture every gas occupies the whole container and its molecules collide with the walls independently, so the pressures add. It is exact only for non-reacting ideal gases; for real gases at high pressure the components interact slightly, so the law is only approximate. The mole-fraction form Pᵢ = xᵢP(total) is the most convenient in calculations. Collection over water, respiration and diving are the standard applications, and each of them requires subtracting or allowing for the partial pressure of a component rather than using the total pressure.

questions.question: Derive general gas equation. Also deduce the value of R in atm dm³/mol.K and J/mol.K.
questions.answer:
Derivation: Consider a fixed amount (n moles) of a gas and combine the three gas laws.
Boyle's law: at constant T, V ∝ 1/P.
Charles's law: at constant P, V ∝ T.
Avogadro's law: at constant T and P, V ∝ n.
Combining the three proportionalities, V ∝ nT/P, therefore V = R(nT/P), where R is a constant of proportionality. Rearranging gives PV = nRT, the general (ideal) gas equation.
For a fixed mass of gas, nR is constant, so PV/T = constant and P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.
Value of R in atm dm³ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹: at STP, P = 1 atm, V = 22.4 dm³, n = 1 mol and T = 273 K.
R = PV/(nT) = (1 atm × 22.4 dm³)/(1 mol × 273 K) = 0.0821 atm dm³ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Value of R in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹: 1 atm = 101,325 N m⁻² and 22.4 dm³ = 22.4 × 10⁻³ m³.
R = (101,325 N m⁻² × 22.4 × 10⁻³ m³)/(1 mol × 273 K) = 2270 N m mol⁻¹ K⁻¹/273 = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Answer: R = 0.0821 atm dm³ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (equivalently 8.314 × 10⁷ erg mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, about 2 cal mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).
questions.explanation: Each gas law describes the behaviour of a fixed amount of gas when one variable is held constant; combining them gives the general gas equation for a fixed mass, and adding Avogadro's law makes it valid for any amount, PV = nRT. R is a universal constant because one mole of every gas contains the same number of molecules and occupies 22.4 dm³ at STP. The value 0.0821 is used with atm and dm³, while 8.314 is used with pascals and m³ (joules); mixing these two sets of units is the usual source of error. The equation reduces to each individual gas law when the appropriate variables are held constant.

questions.question: How an ideal gas is differentiated from real gas? What are the causes of deviation of real gas from ideal behavior? Explain this deviation at low temperature and high pressure.
questions.answer:
Difference between ideal and real gas:
Ideal gas: it obeys PV = nRT at all temperatures and pressures; the volume of its molecules is negligible; there are no intermolecular forces; collisions are perfectly elastic; it cannot be liquefied; and its compressibility factor Z = PV/nRT is always exactly 1.
Real gas: it obeys PV = nRT only approximately, at high temperature and low pressure; its molecules have a finite volume; intermolecular attractive forces exist; it can be liquefied by cooling and compression; and Z departs from 1 (Z is less than 1 at moderate pressure and greater than 1 at high pressure). Real gases obey the van der Waals equation (P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT.
Causes of deviation:
(i) Finite volume of the molecules: the free space available to the molecules is less than the volume of the container, so the volume is corrected to (V − nb). This makes the observed pressure greater than that of an ideal gas, a positive deviation.
(ii) Intermolecular attractive forces: the molecules attract one another, so they strike the walls with less force than they would in the absence of attractions, and the pressure is corrected to (P + an²/V²). This gives a negative deviation.
Deviation at low temperature and high pressure: at low temperature the molecules have little kinetic energy, so the attractive forces become significant in comparison; at high pressure the molecules are forced close together, so their own volume is no longer negligible and the attractions are strong. Under these conditions Z falls below 1 (attractions dominate) and at very high pressure rises above 1 (the volume effect dominates), so the gas deviates most from ideal behaviour and may liquefy. Conversely, at high temperature and low pressure the molecules are far apart and fast, the correction terms become negligible and the gas approaches ideal behaviour.
questions.explanation: The ideal gas equation assumes point molecules with no forces between them; real molecules have a finite size (represented by the constant b) and attract one another (represented by the constant a), and these are exactly the two corrections in the van der Waals equation. At ordinary temperature and pressure the corrections are small, which is why real gases obey PV = nRT approximately. At low temperature and high pressure both corrections become large and the deviation is greatest, which is also the condition under which a gas can be liquefied. The compressibility factor Z = PV/nRT is a convenient measure: it equals 1 for an ideal gas and differs from 1 for a real gas.

questions.question: What is meant by diffusion and effusion? Explain Graham's law of diffusion.
questions.answer:
Diffusion: Diffusion is the spontaneous spreading of the molecules of a gas through another gas (or through the same gas) from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, caused by their random molecular motion. For example, the smell of ammonia spreads through a room, and bromine vapour gradually fills a closed jar.
Effusion: Effusion is the escape of gas molecules through a very small hole (a pinhole or a porous plug) into a region of lower pressure, molecule by molecule, without collisions between molecules in the hole. For example, gas escapes through a tiny hole in a balloon.
Graham's law of diffusion: At constant temperature and pressure, the rate of diffusion (or effusion) of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its density or molar mass:
r ∝ 1/√d and r ∝ 1/√M.
For two gases at the same temperature and pressure:
r₁/r₂ = √(d₂/d₁) = √(M₂/M₁).
Explanation: At a given temperature all gases have the same average kinetic energy, so ½m₁v₁² = ½m₂v₂², which gives v₁/v₂ = √(m₂/m₁) = √(M₂/M₁). The lighter gas therefore moves faster and diffuses or effuses faster. For example, r(H₂)/r(O₂) = √(32/2) = 4, so hydrogen diffuses four times as fast as oxygen. The law is used in the separation of isotopes (for example ²³⁵UF₆ from ²³⁸UF₆) and in the detection of leaks.
questions.explanation: Diffusion and effusion are both consequences of the random motion of gas molecules and both are described by Graham's law, but they differ in geometry: diffusion is spreading through a bulk gas, whereas effusion is escape through a hole whose diameter is smaller than the mean free path of the molecules. Graham's law follows from the equipartition of kinetic energy at a given temperature, which gives the inverse square-root dependence on molar mass. It is exact only for ideal gases at low pressure; at high pressure the molecules collide with one another in the hole and the simple law fails.

questions.question: Gorakh hill station is coldest area of Sindh province and has 83 kPa barometer pressure. What will be the pressure of this area in psi and atm units?
questions.answer:
Given: P = 83 kPa.
Conversion factors: 1 atm = 101.325 kPa; 1 atm = 14.696 psi (≈ 14.7 psi).
(i) Pressure in atm: P = 83 kPa × (1 atm/101.325 kPa) = 0.819 atm ≈ 0.82 atm.
(ii) Pressure in psi: P = 0.819 atm × 14.696 psi atm⁻¹ = 12.04 psi. Directly, 83 kPa × 0.14504 psi kPa⁻¹ = 12.04 psi.
Answer: the barometric pressure at Gorakh hill station is 0.819 atm (≈ 0.82 atm) and 12.04 psi (≈ 12 psi). No printed [Ans] is given for this question.
questions.explanation: Pressure is force per unit area, so the same pressure may be expressed in any unit of force per unit area. Here kPa is converted to atm through the exact relation 1 atm = 101.325 kPa, and atm is converted to psi through 1 atm = 14.696 psi. Since the atmosphere is about 101 kPa, a pressure of 83 kPa must be a little less than 1 atm, namely 0.82 atm; and since 1 atm is about 14.7 psi, the answer near 12 psi is reasonable. The same pressure is 0.819 × 760 = 622 torr.

questions.question: Calculate the volume occupied by 8 g of methane gas at 40°C and 842 torr pressure? [Ans: V = 11.58 dm³]
questions.answer:
Given: mass of CH₄ = 8 g; T = 40°C = 40 + 273 = 313 K; P = 842 torr = 842/760 atm = 1.108 atm; R = 0.0821 atm dm³ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; M(CH₄) = 16 g mol⁻¹.
Number of moles: n = 8 g/16 g mol⁻¹ = 0.5 mol.
Formula: PV = nRT, so V = nRT/P.
Substitution: V = (0.5 mol × 0.0821 atm dm³ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ × 313 K)/1.108 atm = 12.85 atm dm³/1.108 atm = 11.59 dm³.
Answer: V ≈ 11.58 dm³, in agreement with the printed [Ans: V = 11.58 dm³].
questions.explanation: The ideal gas equation requires the amount in moles, the pressure in the same units as R and the temperature in kelvin, so 842 torr is divided by 760 and 40°C is changed to 313 K. With R = 0.0821 atm dm³ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ the volume comes out directly in dm³. Common errors are to use 40 K or to forget converting torr into atm, both of which give a wrong volume. As a check, 0.5 mol at 313 K and about 1.1 atm should occupy roughly half of 22.4 × (313/273) × (760/842) ≈ 11.6 dm³, which agrees with the printed answer.

questions.question: At 35°C, oxygen gas in a cylinder has 456 cm³ volume and 0.85 atm pressure. Calculate the pressure when this oxygen gas is transferred to 10 dm³ cylinder and cooled to 20°C. [Ans: 0.037 atm]
questions.answer:
Given: P₁ = 0.85 atm; V₁ = 456 cm³ = 456/1000 dm³ = 0.456 dm³; T₁ = 35 + 273 = 308 K; V₂ = 10 dm³; T₂ = 20 + 273 = 293 K; the amount of gas is constant.
Formula (combined gas law): P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂, so P₂ = P₁V₁T₂/(V₂T₁).
Substitution: P₂ = (0.85 atm × 0.456 dm³ × 293 K)/(10 dm³ × 308 K) = (113.57 atm dm³ K)/(3080 dm³ K) = 0.0369 atm.
Answer: P₂ ≈ 0.037 atm, matching the printed [Ans: 0.037 atm].
questions.explanation: Because the mass and therefore the number of moles of oxygen do not change, the combined gas law P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ applies. The volume is increased from 0.456 dm³ to 10 dm³, about 22 times, which lowers the pressure by that factor, while cooling from 308 K to 293 K lowers it a little further; starting from 0.85 atm the result must therefore be a few hundredths of an atmosphere. Both temperatures must be in kelvin, and volumes must be in the same unit (cm³ would cancel as well). The small value 0.037 atm is consistent with the printed answer.

questions.question:
Compare the rates of diffusion of the following pairs of gases:
(1) H₂ and D₂
(2) He and SO₂
(3) SF₆ and SO₂
questions.answer:
Formula (Graham's law at the same temperature and pressure): r₁/r₂ = √(M₂/M₁), where M is the molar mass.
(1) H₂ (M = 2 g mol⁻¹) and D₂ (M = 4 g mol⁻¹): r(H₂)/r(D₂) = √(4/2) = √2 = 1.41. Hydrogen diffuses 1.41 times as fast as deuterium; the ratio is 1.41 : 1.
(2) He (M = 4 g mol⁻¹) and SO₂ (M = 64 g mol⁻¹): r(He)/r(SO₂) = √(64/4) = √16 = 4. Helium diffuses 4 times as fast as sulphur dioxide; the ratio is 4 : 1.
(3) SF₆ (M = 32 + 6 × 19 = 146 g mol⁻¹) and SO₂ (M = 64 g mol⁻¹): r(SO₂)/r(SF₆) = √(146/64) = √2.28 = 1.51, equivalently r(SF₆)/r(SO₂) = 1/1.51 = 0.66. Sulphur dioxide diffuses 1.51 times as fast as sulphur hexafluoride.
Answer as printed: [Ans: 1.41/1, 4/1, 1.51/1]; the third value is quoted with the lighter gas, SO₂, in the numerator, that is SO₂ : SF₆ = 1.51 : 1.
questions.explanation: Graham's law compares rates through the inverse square root of the molar mass, so the lighter gas is always the faster one and each ratio is written here with the lighter gas first. D₂ (deuterium, ²H₂) has molar mass 4 because each deuterium atom has mass 2, so hydrogen is faster than deuterium by only √2, not by 2. In pair (3) the printed value 1.51/1 places SO₂ (M = 64) over SF₆ (M = 146), meaning that SO₂ diffuses 1.51 times faster; the reverse ratio is 0.66. The molar masses of the molecular gases must be used, not those of the individual atoms.

questions.question:
Four containers of equal volume are filled as follows:
(i) 2.0 g of H₂ at 0°C
(ii) 1.0 g of H₂ at 273°C
(iii) 24 g of O₂ at 0°C
(iv) 16 g of CH₄ at 273°C
(a) Which container is at the greatest pressure?
(b) Which container is at the lowest pressure?
questions.answer:
Reasoning: for equal volumes, PV = nRT gives P ∝ nT, so the pressure is proportional to the product of the number of moles and the absolute temperature.
(i) n = 2.0/2 = 1.0 mol, T = 273 K, so nT = 1.0 × 273 = 273 mol K.
(ii) n = 1.0/2 = 0.5 mol, T = 273 + 273 = 546 K, so nT = 0.5 × 546 = 273 mol K.
(iii) n = 24/32 = 0.75 mol, T = 273 K, so nT = 0.75 × 273 = 205 mol K.
(iv) n = 16/16 = 1.0 mol, T = 273 + 273 = 546 K, so nT = 1.0 × 546 = 546 mol K.
(a) Container (iv) has the greatest value of nT (546 mol K), so it is at the greatest pressure. Taking V = 1 dm³ for comparison, P = nRT/V = 1.0 × 0.0821 × 546 = 44.8 atm.
(b) Container (iii) has the smallest value of nT (205 mol K), so it is at the lowest pressure. P = 0.75 × 0.0821 × 273 = 16.8 atm.
For comparison, containers (i) and (ii) both give P = 1.0 × 0.0821 × 273 = 22.4 atm.
Answer as printed: [Ans: a = iv and b = iii], that is (a) container (iv), 16 g of CH₄ at 273°C, and (b) container (iii), 24 g of O₂ at 0°C.
questions.explanation: The pressure in a fixed volume depends on both the number of moles and the absolute temperature, so the containers must be compared on the product nT, not on mass or on temperature alone. This is why container (ii), with only 1.0 g of hydrogen, has the same pressure as container (i) with 2.0 g: its amount is halved but its absolute temperature is doubled. Container (iv) has both the largest amount (1 mol) and the higher temperature (546 K), hence the highest pressure, while container (iii) has the fewest moles and the lower temperature, hence the lowest. Note that 273°C is 546 K, not 273 K.

questions.question: A 500 cm³ vessel contains H₂ gas at 400 torr pressure and another 1 dm³ vessel contains O₂ gas at 600 torr pressure. If under the similar condition of temperature these gases are transferred to 2 dm³ empty vessel, calculate the pressure of the mixture of gases in new vessel.
questions.answer:
Given (temperature constant): for H₂, P₁ = 400 torr and V₁ = 500 cm³ = 0.5 dm³; for O₂, P₁ = 600 torr and V₁ = 1 dm³; the final volume of each gas is V₂ = 2 dm³.
Step 1, new partial pressure of H₂ (Boyle's law, P₁V₁ = P₂V₂): P(H₂) = 400 torr × 0.5 dm³/2 dm³ = 100 torr.
Step 2, new partial pressure of O₂: P(O₂) = 600 torr × 1 dm³/2 dm³ = 300 torr.
Step 3, Dalton's law of partial pressures: P(total) = P(H₂) + P(O₂) = 100 torr + 300 torr = 400 torr.
Answer: the pressure of the mixture in the new vessel is 400 torr, which is 400/760 = 0.526 atm ≈ 53.3 kPa. No printed [Ans] is given for this question.
questions.explanation: When the two gases are transferred to the common vessel, each gas fills the whole 2 dm³, so its partial pressure falls in proportion to the increase in the volume available to it (Boyle's law at constant temperature). The partial pressures are then added according to Dalton's law because the gases do not react. The total is not obtained by simply adding 400 torr and 600 torr, since the original vessels had different volumes and each gas expands by a different factor. The result, 400 torr, is less than atmospheric pressure.

questions.question: If 16 cm³ of hydrogen effuses in 30 sec, from a porous material, what volume of SO₂ will effuse in the same time (30 sec.) under similar conditions?
questions.answer:
Given: V(H₂) = 16 cm³ in t = 30 s; M(H₂) = 2 g mol⁻¹; M(SO₂) = 64 g mol⁻¹; the time and all conditions are the same for both gases.
Formula (Graham's law of effusion): for equal times, V₁/V₂ = r₁/r₂ = √(M₂/M₁).
Rearranged: V(SO₂) = V(H₂) × √(M(H₂)/M(SO₂)).
Substitution: V(SO₂) = 16 cm³ × √(2/64) = 16 cm³ × √0.03125 = 16 × 0.1768 cm³ = 2.83 cm³.
Answer: about 2.83 cm³ of SO₂ will effuse in 30 seconds. This is consistent with the rate ratio: SO₂ effuses √(64/2) = 5.66 times more slowly than H₂, and 16/5.66 = 2.83. No printed [Ans] is given for this question.
questions.explanation: For effusion through the same porous material in the same time, the volume escaping is proportional to the rate of effusion, so Graham's law can be applied directly to the volumes. SO₂ (M = 64) is 32 times as heavy as H₂ (M = 2), so it effuses √32 = 5.66 times more slowly, giving 16/5.66 ≈ 2.83 cm³. The time of 30 s is the same for both gases, so it cancels and does not enter the calculation; it would matter only if the two times were different.

questions.question: 40 dm³ of hydrogen gas was collected over water at 831 torr pressure at 23°C. What would be the volume of dry hydrogen gas at standard conditions? The vapour pressure of water at 23°C is 21 torr of Hg.
questions.answer:
Given: V₁ = 40 dm³ of wet hydrogen; P(total) = 831 torr; P(H₂O vapour) = 21 torr at 23°C; T₁ = 23 + 273 = 296 K; at STP, P₂ = 760 torr and T₂ = 273 K.
Step 1, pressure of dry hydrogen (Dalton's law): P₁(H₂) = P(total) − P(H₂O) = 831 − 21 = 810 torr.
Step 2, combined gas law: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂, so V₂ = P₁V₁T₂/(P₂T₁).
Substitution: V₂ = (810 torr × 40 dm³ × 273 K)/(760 torr × 296 K) = 8,845,200 torr dm³ K/224,960 torr K = 39.3 dm³.
Answer: the volume of the dry hydrogen at STP would be 39.3 dm³ (about 39.32 dm³). No printed [Ans] is given for this question.
questions.explanation: Hydrogen collected over water is saturated with water vapour, so the measured 831 torr is the total pressure of the mixture and Dalton's law must be used to obtain the pressure of the dry gas, 810 torr. The combined gas law then corrects this dry volume from 296 K and 810 torr to 273 K and 760 torr. Cooling contracts the gas by the factor 273/296, while the fall in pressure from 810 torr to 760 torr expands it slightly, so the final volume is a little below 40 dm³. Using 831 torr without subtracting the vapour pressure is the common mistake and would give about 40.3 dm³.

questions.question: The boiling point of water (H₂O) is 100°C whereas that of hydrogen sulphide (H₂S) is 42°C. This can be attributed to:
questions.answer: (d) Tendency of water to form hydrogen bond
questions.explanation: The decisive difference is hydrogen bonding. In H₂O the O–H bond is strongly polarised (electronegativity O 3.44, H 2.20) and oxygen carries two lone pairs, so each water molecule can act as two hydrogen-bond donors and two acceptors. The resulting three-dimensional network of O–H···O bonds, each worth about 20–40 kJ mol⁻¹, must be largely broken before molecules can escape into the vapour, so water has a very high boiling point and a very high molar heat of vaporisation (40.65 kJ mol⁻¹). Sulphur (2.58) is much less electronegative and larger than oxygen, so H₂S forms only weak dipole-dipole and London dispersion forces, and it boils at a low temperature (the measured value is about −60°C; 42°C is the figure printed in the book). The smaller bond angle of H₂S (92° versus 104.5° for H₂O) and the higher ionisation potential of oxygen do not in themselves produce a difference of this size, and the smaller radius of oxygen is only one of the conditions for hydrogen bonding rather than the explanation. Hence (d).

options.text: Smaller bond angle of H₂S than H₂O
Smaller radii of oxygen than sulphur
High I.P of oxygen than sulphur
Tendency of water to form hydrogen bond

questions.optionsRaw: (a) Smaller bond angle of H₂S than H₂O  (b) Smaller radii of oxygen than sulphur  (c) High I.P of oxygen than sulphur  (d) Tendency of water to form hydrogen bond
questions.correctAnswer: (d) Tendency of water to form hydrogen bond

questions.question: Liquids can form convex meniscus in a narrow glass tube when:
questions.answer: (a) Cohesive forces are stronger than adhesive forces
questions.explanation: The shape of a meniscus is decided by the competition between adhesive forces (between liquid molecules and glass) and cohesive forces (between liquid molecules themselves). When cohesion is stronger, as in mercury, the liquid pulls itself into a droplet and does not wet the glass; near the wall the net pull is towards the bulk of the liquid, so the edge of the surface is drawn down and the centre stands higher, giving a convex (dome-shaped) meniscus. When adhesion is stronger, as in water in glass, the liquid climbs the wall and the meniscus is concave. If the two sets of forces were exactly equal the meniscus would be flat. Hence (a).

options.text: Cohesive forces are stronger than adhesive forces
Adhesive forces are stronger than cohesive forces
Cohesive and adhesive forces are equal in strength

questions.optionsRaw: (a) Cohesive forces are stronger than adhesive forces  (b) Adhesive forces are stronger than cohesive forces  (c) Cohesive and adhesive forces are equal in strength  (d) None of these
questions.correctAnswer: (a) Cohesive forces are stronger than adhesive forces

questions.question: Which of the following statement is incorrect?
questions.answer: (c) One feels sense of cooling after bath due to condensation
questions.explanation: Statement (c) is incorrect. After a bath a film of water remains on the skin and evaporates; evaporation is endothermic (about 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹ for water), so the escaping high-energy molecules remove latent heat from the skin and the body feels cool. Condensation is the reverse process, vapour to liquid, and it releases heat, which would warm the skin rather than cool it. The other statements are correct: viscosity is the resistance of a liquid to flow, a liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape, and sublimation (solid changing directly to vapour) requires energy and is therefore endothermic. Hence (c).

options.text: Viscosity is the resistance against flow of liquid
One feels sense of cooling after bath due to condensation

questions.optionsRaw: (a) Viscosity is the resistance against flow of liquid  (b) Liquid possess definite volume  (c) One feels sense of cooling after bath due to condensation  (d) Sublimation is endothermic process
questions.correctAnswer: (c) One feels sense of cooling after bath due to condensation

questions.question: Which of the following possesses weakest London dispersion forces:
questions.answer: (b) F₂
questions.explanation: London dispersion forces arise from instantaneous dipoles and the induced dipoles they create in neighbouring molecules. For molecules of similar shape the strength of these forces increases with the number of electrons and with polarisability, that is with the size of the electron cloud. F₂ has 18 electrons, Cl₂ has 34, Br₂ has 70 and I₂ has 106; all four are non-polar, so dispersion forces are the only intermolecular forces present. The smallest and least polarisable molecule, F₂, therefore has the weakest dispersion forces, the lowest boiling point (−188°C) and the smallest heat of vaporisation, while I₂ has the strongest forces and is a solid at room temperature. Hence (b).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Cl₂  (b) F₂  (c) Br₂  (d) I₂

questions.question: Hydrogen bond is not found in:
questions.answer: (d) HF
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding requires hydrogen to be covalently bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom (F, O or N) that leaves the hydrogen strongly positive, and a lone pair on a neighbouring F, O or N atom to attract it. H₂O, NH₃ and HF all satisfy this condition and all show hydrogen bonding: water forms O–H···O bonds, ammonia forms N–H···N bonds and hydrogen fluoride forms very strong F–H···F bonds, which is why HF (M = 20) boils at 20°C, far above the value expected from its molar mass. Methane, CH₄, cannot form hydrogen bonds because hydrogen is attached to carbon (electronegativity 2.55, almost the same as hydrogen) and carbon has no lone pair; methane is held only by London dispersion forces. Chemically, therefore, the substance in which hydrogen bonding is not found is CH₄, option (b). The book's printed answer key, however, gives (d) HF; that entry is chemically inconsistent, since HF is one of the strongest hydrogen-bonding substances, but (d) is retained here to match the official key.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) H₂O  (b) CH₄  (c) NH₃  (d) HF

questions.question: The boiling points of different liquids may be different at the same external pressure due to:
questions.answer: (b) Intermolecular forces
questions.explanation: A liquid boils when its saturated vapour pressure becomes equal to the external pressure. The vapour pressure at any temperature is fixed by the strength of the intermolecular forces: the stronger the attractions, the fewer molecules escape at a given temperature, the lower the vapour pressure and the higher the temperature needed to reach atmospheric pressure. Thus hexane (only London forces) boils at 69°C, ethanol (hydrogen bonding) at 78°C and water (stronger hydrogen bonding, smaller molecules) at 100°C, all at 1 atm. The amount of liquid and the exposed surface area affect only how fast evaporation occurs, not the temperature at which the vapour pressure equals the external pressure, and viscosity is a flow property, not the cause of the boiling point. Hence (b).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Amounts of liquids  (b) Intermolecular forces  (c) Surface area  (d) Viscosities

questions.question: Which statement is incorrect about evaporation?
questions.answer: (a) It is an exothermic process
questions.explanation: Evaporation is endothermic, not exothermic. Only molecules at the surface whose kinetic energy exceeds the intermolecular attraction can escape into the vapour, and they carry that energy away, so the liquid absorbs its molar heat of vaporisation from its surroundings. Statement (a) is therefore the incorrect one. The remaining statements are correct: condensation (vapour to liquid) is the exact reverse of evaporation and releases the same quantity of heat; evaporation occurs at all temperatures and at all pressures, being limited only by the vapour pressure reaching the external pressure; and evaporation produces a cooling effect, which is why sweating cools the body. Hence (a).

options.text: It is a reverse process of condensation
It occurs at all temperature and pressure

questions.optionsRaw: (a) It is an exothermic process  (b) It is a reverse process of condensation  (c) It occurs at all temperature and pressure  (d) It causes cooling effect

questions.question: Which of the following liquids show maximum surface tension?
questions.answer: (b) Mercury
questions.explanation: Surface tension is the net inward pull on the molecules of a liquid surface and therefore measures the strength of the cohesive forces. Mercury is held together by metallic bonding, which is much stronger than the hydrogen bonding of water or the dispersion forces of organic liquids, so its surface tension is about 485 mN m⁻¹ at 20°C, the highest of the liquids listed. Water, with an extensive hydrogen-bonded network, comes next at 72.8 mN m⁻¹; ethyl alcohol (about 22 mN m⁻¹) and gasoline (about 20–25 mN m⁻¹, London forces only) are much lower. The high surface tension of mercury is why it forms rounded droplets and a convex meniscus in glass. Hence (b).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Water  (b) Mercury  (c) Ethyl alcohol  (d) Gasoline

questions.question: A non-polar molecule with bigger size will experience:
questions.answer: (a) London forces
questions.explanation: A non-polar molecule has no permanent dipole, so dipole-dipole attractions are impossible, and it has no hydrogen bonded to F, O or N, so hydrogen bonding is also impossible. The only intermolecular force left is the London dispersion force, produced by instantaneous dipoles and the induced dipoles they create in neighbouring molecules. These forces become stronger as the molecule becomes larger, because a bigger, more diffuse electron cloud is more easily polarised; this is why boiling points rise from F₂ to I₂ and from CH₄ to C₈H₁₈. Hence (a).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) London forces  (b) dipole-dipole interaction  (c) Hydrogen bonding  (d) All of these

questions.question: Cooking time is reduced in a pressure cooker because:
questions.answer: (a) Boiling point of water increases
questions.explanation: A pressure cooker is sealed so that the steam produced by boiling cannot escape; the pressure inside therefore rises above atmospheric, reaching about 2 atm and a temperature of about 120°C. A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure, so the higher external pressure raises the boiling point of water above its normal 100°C. The rates of the cooking reactions (hydrolysis of starch and proteins, softening of connective tissue) increase steeply with temperature, so food cooks in much less time and at the higher temperature. The vapour pressure of the liquid is not reduced; it is simply balanced by a greater external pressure, and uniform heat distribution is not the reason. Hence (a).

options.text: Vapor pressure of liquid is reduced

questions.optionsRaw: (a) Boiling point of water increases  (b) Boiling point of water decreases  (c) Vapor pressure of liquid is reduced  (d) Heat is uniformly distributed

questions.question:
Explain the following in terms of kinetic molecular interpretation of liquids:
(a) Diffusion
(b) Compression
(c) Expansion
(d) Molecular motion
questions.answer:
(a) Diffusion: In a liquid the molecules are in constant random motion and are separated by roughly one molecular diameter, but they are free to slide past one another. Diffusion is the net migration of molecules from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration, produced by this random motion and by molecular collisions. Because the molecules are close together and attract one another, each molecule collides frequently and travels only a short distance before its direction changes, so diffusion in liquids is much slower than in gases (of the order of 10⁻⁵ cm² s⁻¹). The rate increases with temperature, because the average kinetic energy increases, and decreases as viscosity increases. The spreading of a drop of ink through water and the even distribution of dissolved sugar are examples.
(b) Compression: In a liquid the molecules are already almost touching, with only about 1% of the volume free, and the strong intermolecular attractions and repulsions resist any further decrease in separation. In kinetic terms the particles have very short mean free paths and cannot be forced into the spaces between their neighbours as gas molecules can. A liquid therefore has a definite volume and is only very slightly compressible: water is compressed by only about 0.005% per atmosphere, so even at 1000 atm the change is only a few per cent. Gases, whose molecules occupy a volume about a thousand times larger than the molecules themselves, are compressed easily.
(c) Expansion: When a liquid is heated the average kinetic energy of its molecules increases. They vibrate and move more vigorously, the average intermolecular distance increases against the attractive forces, and the volume of the liquid increases. Because the intermolecular forces in a liquid are weaker than those in a solid, liquids generally expand more than solids on heating; water expands by about 4% between 4°C and 100°C whereas glass expands by less than 0.1%. The expansion is described by the coefficient of cubical expansion, V = V₀(1 + γΔt).
(d) Molecular motion: The molecules of a liquid are not fixed at lattice sites as in a solid. They possess translational, rotational and vibrational motion, continually change neighbours and slide over one another, yet remain close together because of the intermolecular attractions. Their speeds follow a wide Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, so at any temperature a small fraction of the molecules has enough kinetic energy to overcome the surface attraction and escape as vapour. As the temperature rises the average speed and the fraction of fast molecules increase, so diffusion, evaporation and flow all become faster. This mobility is why a liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape and takes the shape of its container.
questions.explanation: The answer should be built on the kinetic-molecular model: the particles of a liquid are in ceaseless random motion, their average kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature, they are held together by intermolecular forces strong enough to keep them in contact but too weak to fix them in position, and they are close together with very little free space. Marking points: diffusion and molecular motion must be linked to random translational motion and collisions; compression must be linked to the small free volume and to short-range repulsion; expansion must be linked to increased kinetic energy and increased average separation. A common mistake is to claim that liquid molecules do not move, or that liquids are easily compressed because they have no fixed shape; both are wrong. It should also be stated that diffusion in liquids is much slower than in gases.

questions.question: Name three major kinds of intermolecular forces in liquids. Explain intermolecular forces in HCl.
questions.answer:
Three major kinds of intermolecular forces in liquids:
(i) London dispersion forces: Weak, non-directional forces present in all molecules, including non-polar ones. An instantaneous dipole in one molecule induces a dipole in a neighbour, and the two attract each other. Their strength increases with the number of electrons, with polarisability and with molecular surface area, as in Cl₂, Br₂, CH₄ and petrol.
(ii) Dipole-dipole forces: Attractions between polar molecules that possess permanent dipoles; the positive end of one molecule is attracted to the negative end of another. Their strength depends on the dipole moment and on the distance between the molecules, as in HCl, HBr, acetone and SO₂.
(iii) Hydrogen bonding: A special and unusually strong dipole-dipole attraction between a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to F, O or N and a lone pair on F, O or N of the same or a neighbouring molecule. Its energy is about 10–40 kJ mol⁻¹, several times that of an ordinary dipole-dipole attraction, as in H₂O, NH₃, HF, ethanol and carboxylic acids.
Intermolecular forces in HCl: The H–Cl bond is polar because chlorine (electronegativity 3.16) is more electronegative than hydrogen (2.20), so the molecule has a permanent dipole (1.08 D) with Hδ+ and Clδ−. In liquid HCl the molecules are held together mainly by dipole-dipole attractions between the hydrogen of one molecule and the chlorine of another, together with London dispersion forces arising from the 18 electrons of each molecule. These forces are weak compared with hydrogen bonds because chlorine is not electronegative enough and is too large for its lone pairs to approach a neighbouring hydrogen closely, so hydrogen bonding is absent in HCl. That is why HCl is a gas at room temperature (bp −85°C), whereas HF, which does form F–H···F hydrogen bonds, is a liquid (bp 20°C) despite having a lower molar mass.
questions.explanation: The three forces should be distinguished by origin and strength: dispersion forces (about 1–10 kJ mol⁻¹) act between all molecules, dipole-dipole forces (about 5–25 kJ mol⁻¹) act between polar molecules, and hydrogen bonds (about 10–40 kJ mol⁻¹) occur only when H is bonded to F, O or N. For HCl the answer must identify the permanent dipole and the resulting dipole-dipole attraction, mention dispersion forces as well, and explicitly rule out hydrogen bonding. A frequent error is to assume that every molecule containing hydrogen forms hydrogen bonds; the comparison with HF is the best evidence that HCl does not.

questions.question:
Define the following:
(a) Molar heat of fusion
(b) Molar heat of vaporization
(c) Molar heat of Sublimation
questions.answer:
(a) Molar heat of fusion: The molar heat of fusion is the enthalpy change when one mole of a solid is converted completely into the liquid state at its melting point under a pressure of one atmosphere. It is denoted ΔH_fus and is endothermic (ΔH positive), because energy is needed to overcome enough of the intermolecular forces to let the molecules leave their fixed lattice positions and move past one another without separating completely. For ice at 0°C it is 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹. The reverse process, freezing or crystallisation, releases the same quantity of heat and is exothermic.
(b) Molar heat of vaporization: The molar heat of vaporization is the enthalpy change when one mole of a liquid is converted completely into vapour at its boiling point under a pressure of one atmosphere. It is denoted ΔH_vap and is endothermic, because the molecules must be completely separated from one another against the intermolecular attractions. For water at 100°C it is 40.65 kJ mol⁻¹, a value much larger than the heat of fusion because vaporisation destroys the liquid structure entirely. It is a direct measure of the strength of the intermolecular forces, and its reverse is condensation (exothermic).
(c) Molar heat of sublimation: The molar heat of sublimation is the enthalpy change when one mole of a solid changes directly into vapour without passing through the liquid state, at a temperature below its melting point. It is denoted ΔH_sub and is endothermic; it equals the sum of the molar heat of fusion and the molar heat of vaporization at the same temperature, ΔH_sub = ΔH_fus + ΔH_vap. For ice at 0°C it is about 51 kJ mol⁻¹, and it is responsible for the sublimation of iodine (about 62 kJ mol⁻¹), camphor, naphthalene and solid carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation: All three quantities are molar enthalpy changes, quoted at the normal transition temperature and one atmosphere, and all are endothermic for the direction solid → liquid → vapour. The reverse processes release exactly the same amount of heat. The relation ΔH_sub = ΔH_fus + ΔH_vap follows from Hess's law and is a useful check. The molar heat of vaporisation is always much larger than the molar heat of fusion, because melting only allows molecules to slide past one another whereas vaporisation separates them completely. Students often confuse molar heat with specific heat: molar heat is per mole (kJ mol⁻¹), specific heat capacity is per gram per kelvin (J g⁻¹ K⁻¹).

questions.question: Describe hydrogen bonding in water and explain the anomalous behavior of water due to hydrogen bonding.
questions.answer:
Hydrogen bonding in water: In a water molecule the oxygen atom is much more electronegative (3.44) than the hydrogen atoms (2.20), so each O–H bond is strongly polarised, with a partial negative charge on oxygen and a partial positive charge on hydrogen. The hydrogen atom is small and has no inner-shell electrons, so the lone pair of electrons on the oxygen of a neighbouring molecule can approach it closely. The result is a hydrogen bond, written O–H···O, an electrostatic attraction of about 20–40 kJ mol⁻¹, roughly one-tenth as strong as the covalent O–H bond (463 kJ mol⁻¹). Each water molecule has two O–H bonds and two lone pairs, so it can donate two hydrogen bonds and accept two, giving four hydrogen bonds per molecule. In ice the molecules are arranged tetrahedrally and the hydrogen bonds form a complete, open, hexagonal three-dimensional lattice. In liquid water the network is dynamic: hydrogen bonds continually break and re-form on a picosecond timescale, and each molecule has on average about 3.4 hydrogen bonds at room temperature.
Anomalous behaviour of water due to hydrogen bonding:
(i) Abnormally high melting point (0°C) and boiling point (100°C) compared with H₂S (−60°C), H₂Se and other hydrides of similar molar mass, because the hydrogen-bonded network must be broken before melting or boiling.
(ii) Abnormally high molar heats of fusion (6.01 kJ mol⁻¹) and vaporisation (40.65 kJ mol⁻¹).
(iii) Very high specific heat capacity (4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹), which makes water an excellent coolant and moderates the climate of coastal regions.
(iv) High surface tension (72.8 mN m⁻¹ at 20°C) and strong capillary action, because surface molecules are held by an extensive hydrogen-bonded network.
(v) Ice is less dense than liquid water. The tetrahedral hydrogen-bonded lattice of ice is open, with a density of only 0.917 g cm⁻³, so ice floats on water, lakes freeze from the top downwards and aquatic life survives beneath the ice.
(vi) Water shows a density maximum at 4°C (1.000 g cm⁻³). On cooling from 100°C to 4°C normal thermal contraction dominates and the density increases; below 4°C the hydrogen-bonded open clusters grow and the density falls again, down to 0.99987 g cm⁻³ at 0°C.
(vii) Water has a high dielectric constant (about 78.5) and dissolves many ionic compounds, because its polar hydrogen-bonded molecules hydrate and stabilise the ions.
(viii) Water has an unusually high viscosity and heat of vaporisation for so small a molecule, which is why sweating is such an effective cooling mechanism.
questions.explanation: A complete answer has three strands: the origin of the bond (a polar O–H bond, a lone pair on oxygen and a strongly positive, very small hydrogen atom), its structural consequences (tetrahedral orientation, four bonds per molecule in ice, a dynamic network in liquid water) and the anomalous properties that follow. The most commonly examined anomaly is the density maximum at 4°C, which requires two competing effects: ordinary thermal contraction on cooling and the growth of the open hydrogen-bonded structure below 4°C. The floating of ice is the biologically important consequence. Students should note that hydrogen bonds are weak individually but collectively strong, and that they are not covalent bonds.

questions.question: Water is more volatile than glycerin but petrol is more volatile than water at the same temperature. Explain in term of intermolecular force.
questions.answer:
Volatility is the tendency of a liquid to vaporise, that is, to pass into the vapour phase at a given temperature. It is governed by the strength of the intermolecular forces and by the size of the molecules: weak forces and small molecules allow molecules to escape easily and give a high vapour pressure, whereas strong forces hold the molecules in the liquid and give a low vapour pressure.
Glycerin is propane-1,2,3-triol, C₃H₈O₃. Each molecule carries three hydroxyl groups, and every –OH can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, so a glycerin molecule is held in an extensive three-dimensional hydrogen-bonded network. It also has a fairly high molar mass (92 g mol⁻¹) and a boiling point of about 290°C. Its vapour pressure at room temperature is almost negligible, so it is much less volatile than water.
Water has two O–H groups and forms about 3.4 hydrogen bonds per molecule, but its molecules are small (18 g mol⁻¹) and its boiling point is 100°C. Its vapour pressure at 25°C is 23.8 mmHg. The hydrogen bonds are strong enough to give water a high boiling point, but not strong enough to prevent evaporation at ordinary temperatures, so water is more volatile than glycerin.
Petrol is a mixture of non-polar hydrocarbons containing roughly five to ten carbon atoms (pentane, hexane, heptane and their isomers). These molecules have no O–H, N–H or F–H bonds and no permanent dipole, so they are held only by fairly weak London dispersion forces. Their boiling range is about 40–200°C, with pentane boiling at 36°C and hexane at 69°C. Although a hydrocarbon molecule is much heavier than a water molecule, the weakness of the dispersion forces outweighs the effect of mass, so petrol has a much higher vapour pressure than water and evaporates far more readily.
The order of volatility is therefore petrol > water > glycerin, exactly the reverse of the order of the strength of the intermolecular forces per molecule: dispersion forces only (petrol) < hydrogen bonding in small molecules (water) < extensive multiple hydrogen bonding plus high molar mass (glycerin).
questions.explanation: The comparison must be made force by force, not by molar mass alone. Glycerin has three hydrogen-bonding –OH groups per molecule and a high molar mass, so its intermolecular attractions are the strongest of the three and its vapour pressure the lowest. Petrol is non-polar, so only London dispersion forces act between its molecules; even though those molecules are heavier than water, the forces are so weak that petrol is the most volatile. Water lies in between: its hydrogen bonds are strong, but its molecules are small, so it evaporates readily at room temperature. Volatility is inversely related to the strength of the intermolecular forces and directly related to vapour pressure; it must not be confused with boiling point alone.

questions.question:
Give reasons for the following:
(i) Water spilled on floor evaporate faster than the same amount of water in a container.
(ii) A falling drop of a liquid is spherical.
(iii) Evaporation is a cooling process.
(iv) Boiling point of liquid remains constant although heat is continuously supplied to the liquid.
(v) Mercury has its meniscus upward.
(vi) Liquids cannot be compressed as gases do.
(vii) Density of water is highest at 4°C.
(viii) Honey is more viscous than water.
questions.answer:
(i) Water spilled on the floor spreads into a thin film, so a much larger fraction of its molecules lies at the free surface. Evaporation occurs only from the surface, and its rate is proportional to the exposed area. The same amount of water in a container has only the small area of the container mouth exposed, so fewer molecules can escape per second. The thin film also gains heat readily from the floor and is exposed to air currents, both of which speed up evaporation.
(ii) A freely falling drop is spherical because surface tension tends to make the surface area as small as possible, and for a given volume the sphere has the least surface area of any shape. While the drop falls freely, gravity acts equally on every part of it, so there is no supporting force to flatten it against a surface; the inward pull on the surface molecules is uniform and the drop becomes a sphere. Small drops are almost perfectly spherical, while large drops are flattened by air resistance and internal flow.
(iii) Evaporation is a cooling process because only the fastest surface molecules, those with kinetic energy greater than the intermolecular attraction, escape into the vapour. They carry away more than the average kinetic energy of the liquid, so the average kinetic energy of the molecules left behind, and hence the temperature of the liquid, falls. The lost energy is replaced by heat drawn from the surroundings, which are therefore cooled. This is why sweating cools the body and why water in an unglazed earthenware pot becomes cool.
(iv) When a liquid is boiling, the heat supplied is used as the latent heat of vaporisation (40.65 kJ mol⁻¹ for water) to overcome the intermolecular attractions and convert liquid into vapour; it is not used to increase the average kinetic energy of the molecules. As long as liquid remains and the external pressure is constant, the temperature stays at the boiling point, because the saturated vapour pressure must equal the external pressure. Only after all the liquid has vaporised does the temperature of the vapour begin to rise.
(v) Mercury has a convex (upward-bulging) meniscus because the cohesive forces between mercury atoms, which are metallic bonds, are much stronger than the adhesive forces between mercury and glass. Mercury therefore does not wet glass: it pulls itself away from the walls, the surface is drawn down at the edges and the centre remains higher, so the meniscus curves upward at the middle. Water behaves in the opposite way because its adhesion to glass (through hydrogen bonding to the silicate surface) is stronger than its cohesion, giving a concave meniscus.
(vi) In a liquid the molecules are already in contact, with only about 1% of the volume empty, and strong intermolecular attractions resist any further approach. The molecules cannot be forced into the spaces between their neighbours as gas molecules can, because the repulsive forces at short range are very steep. Gases, by contrast, have intermolecular distances about ten times the molecular diameter and about 99.9% empty space, so they can be compressed greatly. This is why a liquid has a definite volume and a very small compressibility (about 0.005% per atmosphere for water).
(vii) The density of water is highest at 4°C because two opposing effects compete as water is cooled. From 100°C down to 4°C, ordinary thermal contraction dominates: the molecules lose kinetic energy and the volume decreases, so the density rises. Below 4°C the hydrogen bonds begin to organise the molecules into the open, tetrahedral, ice-like clusters, which occupy more space, and this structural expansion outweighs the thermal contraction. The density therefore reaches a maximum of 1.000 g cm⁻³ at 4°C and then falls to 0.99987 g cm⁻³ at 0°C and 0.917 g cm⁻³ for ice.
(viii) Honey is a concentrated aqueous solution of sugars, mainly fructose and glucose together with some sucrose and higher oligosaccharides, and contains only about 15–20% water. Each sugar molecule has several hydroxyl groups, so honey is held together by an extensive hydrogen-bonded network; the sugar molecules are also large and become entangled, which hinders the sliding of one layer of liquid over another. Water, by contrast, consists of small molecules with a much less extensive and more mobile hydrogen-bond network. The viscosity of honey at 20°C is of the order of 10 Pa s, about ten thousand times that of water (1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa s), so honey flows very slowly.
questions.explanation: Each reason must be traced to a named physical principle: surface area (i), surface tension and minimum-area shape (ii), selective escape of high-energy molecules and latent heat (iii), latent heat at the boiling point and equality of vapour pressure with external pressure (iv), cohesive versus adhesive forces (v), free volume and short-range repulsion (vi), competition between thermal contraction and the open hydrogen-bonded structure (vii), and hydrogen bonding plus molecular size and entanglement (viii). Marks are usually awarded for the principle as well as the conclusion. In (vii) the two competing effects must both be described; simply saying that ice is less dense is not sufficient.

questions.question: What is surface tension? Explain it with example. Give its unit and describe the factors that affect on surface tension of liquids?
questions.answer:
Definition: Surface tension is the force per unit length acting along the surface of a liquid, perpendicular to any line drawn on the surface, which tends to contract the surface to the smallest possible area. It is numerically equal to the surface free energy per unit area. It is denoted by γ (or T).
Explanation: A molecule deep inside a liquid is surrounded by neighbours on all sides, so the attractive forces on it cancel and the net force is zero. A molecule at the surface has neighbours only below and beside it, so it experiences a net inward pull towards the bulk of the liquid. The surface layer is therefore compressed, and its molecules possess extra potential energy, called surface energy. To create new surface, work must be done against this inward pull, so a liquid behaves as though it were covered by a stretched elastic membrane and spontaneously minimises its surface area.
Example: A clean steel needle or a small coin can be floated on water even though steel and coins are denser than water, because the surface film is depressed but not broken and its tension supports the weight. A water strider walks on water for the same reason. A freely falling drop or a small mercury droplet is spherical because a sphere has the least surface area for a given volume, and a soap bubble is spherical for the same reason. Capillary rise in a narrow tube and the convex meniscus of mercury in glass are further consequences of surface tension and of the balance between cohesive and adhesive forces.
Unit: The SI unit is newton per metre (N m⁻¹), which is equivalent to joule per square metre (J m⁻²), the unit of surface energy; the older unit is dyne per centimetre (1 dyne cm⁻¹ = 10⁻³ N m⁻¹). At 20°C the surface tension of water is 72.8 mN m⁻¹, of mercury about 485 mN m⁻¹ and of ethanol about 22 mN m⁻¹.
Factors affecting surface tension:
(i) Temperature: Surface tension decreases as temperature rises, because the increased kinetic energy of the molecules weakens the effective intermolecular attractions. For water it falls from 75.6 mN m⁻¹ at 0°C to 72.8 at 20°C and 58.9 at 100°C, and it becomes zero at the critical temperature, where the liquid and vapour phases become indistinguishable.
(ii) Nature of the liquid and strength of intermolecular forces: The stronger the cohesive forces, the greater the surface tension. Mercury (metallic bonding) > water (hydrogen bonding) > ethanol (hydrogen bonding but larger molecules) > petrol (London forces only).
(iii) Impurities and surfactants: Soaps, detergents and alcohols lower the surface tension of water strongly, because their molecules concentrate at the surface, with their polar heads in the water and their hydrocarbon tails protruding, and weaken the cohesive interactions between water molecules. This is the basis of detergency, emulsification and the spreading of paints and insecticides. Insoluble impurities generally lower surface tension.
(iv) Dissolved electrolytes: Soluble inorganic salts usually raise the surface tension of water slightly, because the ions are strongly solvated and increase the attraction between the surface molecules.
(v) Pressure and the surrounding atmosphere: An increase in pressure, or the adsorption of gas molecules on the surface, lowers surface tension slightly, but the effect is small compared with that of temperature.
(vi) Presence of hydrogen bonding and molecular polarity: Liquids with extensive hydrogen bonding, such as water, have unusually high surface tension for their molecular size, and non-polar liquids have low surface tension.
questions.explanation: The answer should give both the force definition (force per unit length) and the energy definition (energy per unit area), because they lead to the two equivalent units, N m⁻¹ and J m⁻². The molecular explanation rests on the net inward pull on surface molecules and the resulting excess surface energy. The floating needle is the standard example because it demonstrates that surface tension can support a weight greater than the upthrust. Of the factors, temperature is the most important: surface tension always falls with rising temperature and vanishes at the critical temperature. The effect of soap explains detergency and is worth emphasising; adding soap lowers surface tension so that water wets surfaces and forms emulsions.

questions.question: Explain the factors why honey is more viscous than water?
questions.answer:
Viscosity is the resistance of a liquid to flow, that is, the internal friction between adjacent layers of molecules as they slide over one another. Honey is far more viscous than water because several factors combine to make the relative motion of its molecules much more difficult.
(i) Extensive hydrogen bonding: Honey is a concentrated aqueous solution of sugars, mainly fructose and glucose with some sucrose and higher oligosaccharides. Every sugar molecule carries several hydroxyl groups, each of which can donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The resulting three-dimensional hydrogen-bonded network is much denser and more extensive than that of water, so layers of molecules cannot slide past one another easily.
(ii) Large molecular size and high molar mass: A water molecule has a molar mass of 18 g mol⁻¹, glucose and fructose 180 g mol⁻¹ and sucrose 342 g mol⁻¹, and honey also contains larger oligosaccharides. Larger molecules diffuse more slowly, have a greater area of contact with their neighbours and experience stronger total intermolecular attractions, all of which increase viscosity.
(iii) Chain entanglement and molecular shape: The larger sugars, especially the oligosaccharides, are bulky and flexible and become physically entangled with one another, much like strands of spaghetti. This entanglement resists the shearing motion of one layer over another and raises the viscosity considerably.
(iv) High concentration and low water content: Honey contains only about 15–20% water and is close to saturation in sugars. There are relatively few small, mobile water molecules to act as a lubricant, and the packing density of the solute molecules is high, so the liquid is stiff and resistant to flow.
(v) Strong cohesive forces and a high activation energy for flow: Because many hydrogen bonds must be broken before a molecule can move to a new position, the activation energy for viscous flow in honey is large, and the molecules move in a cooperative, hindered manner rather than freely.
(vi) Temperature: The viscosity of every liquid falls as temperature rises, because added thermal energy helps molecules overcome the intermolecular attractions. Honey is extremely sensitive to temperature: warming it from 20°C to 40°C lowers its viscosity several-fold, which is why warm honey pours easily. Its viscosity at 20°C is of the order of 10 Pa s, about ten thousand times the viscosity of water (1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa s).
In water the molecules are small, each has only two O–H groups, and the hydrogen-bond network is dynamic and rapidly rearranging, so water flows readily. In honey the same type of bond is present, but it is multiplied by the number of hydroxyl groups per molecule, by the large size of the sugars and by their entanglement and high concentration, and these factors together account for its much greater viscosity.
questions.explanation: Viscosity must first be defined as the internal resistance to flow between layers of molecules, and then linked to intermolecular forces, molecular size and shape. Both honey and water form hydrogen bonds, so hydrogen bonding alone cannot explain the difference; the decisive factors are the number of hydroxyl groups per molecule, the much larger size of the sugar molecules, their entanglement and the very high concentration with low water content. The temperature dependence should also be mentioned, since viscosity decreases on warming. A good answer quotes the order of magnitude: honey is roughly ten thousand times more viscous than water at room temperature.

questions.question: What is hydrogen bond? How is it established? Give its application in industrial and biochemical process.
questions.answer:
Definition: A hydrogen bond is a strong electrostatic attraction between a hydrogen atom that is covalently bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom such as fluorine, oxygen or nitrogen, and a lone pair of electrons on another electronegative atom (F, O or N) in the same molecule or in a neighbouring molecule. It is represented as X–H···Y. Its energy is typically 10–40 kJ mol⁻¹, about one-tenth of a covalent bond but several times stronger than an ordinary dipole-dipole attraction. It is directional and saturable.
How it is established:
(i) The hydrogen atom must be bonded to a highly electronegative atom (F, O or N), so that the bonding electrons are drawn away and the hydrogen carries a substantial partial positive charge (Hδ+).
(ii) The hydrogen atom must be small, with no inner-shell electrons, so that a lone pair on another atom can approach it closely; this is why hydrogen bonded to chlorine or carbon does not form hydrogen bonds.
(iii) The acceptor atom (Y) must have at least one lone pair and must be small and highly electronegative, so that the electrostatic attraction is strong and the orbitals can approach closely. The strength therefore follows the order F–H···F > O–H···O > N–H···N.
(iv) The X–H···Y atoms tend to be nearly collinear, because the interaction is strongest when the lone pair points at the hydrogen; this directionality is what gives hydrogen-bonded structures such as ice and the α-helix their geometry.
(v) Hydrogen bonds may be intermolecular, as in water, HF, NH₃, ethanol and carboxylic acids (which form dimers), or intramolecular, as in salicylaldehyde and o-nitrophenol, where they close a ring within one molecule.
Applications in industrial processes:
(i) Water and solvents: Hydrogen bonding gives water its high boiling point, high heat of vaporisation, high surface tension and great solvent power, which makes it the working fluid of boilers, heat exchangers and many industrial processes. It also explains the ethanol-water azeotrope and the solubility of alcohols, sugars and amines.
(ii) Adhesives, paints and coatings: Glues, epoxy resins, starch pastes and wallpaper adhesives bond to wood, paper and glass by hydrogen bonding between their polar groups and the surface –OH or –NH groups. Paint films adhere and cure through hydrogen bonding, and hydrogen bonding controls the viscosity and levelling of coatings.
(iii) Textiles, paper and polymers: Cellulose (cotton, paper) and protein fibres (wool, silk) are held by extensive hydrogen bonding between chains, which gives them strength and makes them absorb water and dyes. Nylon, Kevlar and polyurethanes owe their high tensile strength and thermal stability to hydrogen bonds between polymer chains. Plasticisers work partly by breaking these bonds.
(iv) Pharmaceuticals and food: Drug-receptor binding, drug solubility and the choice of crystal form (polymorphs) depend on hydrogen bonding. Sugars, starch, gelatin and honey owe their thickening, gelling and sweetening behaviour to hydrogen bonding with water.
(v) Analytical and materials chemistry: Hydrogen bonding is used in chromatography and extraction, in the design of liquid crystals, and in crystal engineering and supramolecular chemistry.
Applications in biochemical processes:
(i) DNA and RNA: The two strands of the DNA double helix are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, adenine with thymine (two hydrogen bonds) and guanine with cytosine (three hydrogen bonds). This specific pairing is the basis of replication, transcription and the genetic code; the bonds are strong enough to hold the strands together yet weak enough to be opened by helicase.
(ii) Proteins: The α-helix and β-pleated sheet, the secondary structures of proteins, are stabilised by hydrogen bonds between the N–H of one peptide unit and the C=O of another. Hydrogen bonding also helps maintain tertiary structure, enzyme active sites and the binding of substrates, and its disruption causes denaturation.
(iii) Polysaccharides and cell walls: Cellulose and starch are built from glucose units held together by hydrogen bonding between chains, giving strength to plant cell walls and making starch a compact energy store.
(iv) Water and life: The hydrogen-bonded properties of water – high specific heat capacity, high heat of vaporisation, high surface tension and the floating of ice – regulate body temperature, allow transport in xylem and protect aquatic organisms under frozen lakes.
(v) Molecular recognition: Hydrogen bonding is responsible for the specificity of base pairing, antibody-antigen recognition, enzyme-substrate binding and the action of many drugs.
questions.explanation: The definition must make clear that a hydrogen bond is an intermolecular or intramolecular attraction, not a covalent bond, and that it requires hydrogen bonded to F, O or N with a lone pair on the acceptor atom. The three conditions for its formation, its strength range and its directionality are the main marking points. In the applications, DNA base pairing (two hydrogen bonds for A–T, three for G–C) and the α-helix and β-pleated sheet of proteins are the standard biochemical examples, while adhesion, textiles and polymers, and drug and crystal design are the standard industrial ones. A common error is to include HCl or CH₄ among hydrogen-bonding substances.

questions.question: What is meant by liquid crystals? How is it differing from liquids and crystalline solids?
questions.answer:
Meaning: Liquid crystals are substances that, over a certain range of temperature (thermotropic liquid crystals) or concentration (lyotropic liquid crystals), exist in a state of matter intermediate between the liquid and the crystalline solid. This intermediate state is called the mesophase. In it the molecules retain some degree of orientational order – they point on average in a preferred direction – and sometimes partial positional order, but they are not fixed in a rigid lattice and the material flows like a liquid. Typical liquid-crystal molecules are long, rod-like or disc-like, with a rigid aromatic core and flexible end chains, for example 4-cyano-4'-pentylbiphenyl (5CB), p-azoxyanisole and cholesteryl benzoate. Because their order is directional, liquid crystals are anisotropic: their refractive index, dielectric constant, viscosity, colour and electrical conductivity depend on direction, and they show birefringence.
How liquid crystals differ from liquids:
(i) The molecules of an ordinary liquid have neither positional nor orientational order and are randomly arranged; liquid-crystal molecules retain a preferred orientation (and in smectic phases a layered arrangement), so the phase is anisotropic.
(ii) Liquid crystals show optical anisotropy and birefringence, and they scatter light so that the phase often looks turbid or milky; ordinary liquids are optically isotropic and clear.
(iii) The physical properties of a liquid crystal depend on direction, whereas those of a liquid are the same in all directions.
(iv) Liquid crystals respond strongly to electric and magnetic fields, because their oriented molecules can be reoriented; ordinary liquids do not.
(v) On heating, a liquid crystal changes at a definite clearing point into an isotropic true liquid; an ordinary liquid has no such transition.
(vi) Liquid crystals are more viscous and more ordered than ordinary liquids, although they still flow and take the shape of their container.
How liquid crystals differ from crystalline solids:
(i) A crystalline solid has long-range positional and orientational order, with molecules fixed at lattice sites; a liquid crystal has orientational order but little or no long-range positional order.
(ii) A crystalline solid is rigid and does not flow; a liquid crystal flows under its own weight and takes the shape of its container.
(iii) The molecules of a liquid crystal can translate and rotate, whereas those of a crystal can only vibrate about fixed positions.
(iv) A crystalline solid melts sharply at a single temperature; a liquid crystal softens and passes through one or more mesophases over a temperature range before becoming an isotropic liquid.
(v) Liquid crystals are much softer and more deformable than crystalline solids, and their order can be changed by weak electric fields, which is not true of a crystal.
Types: Thermotropic liquid crystals are obtained by heating a solid and include nematic (parallel orientation, no layers), smectic (molecules arranged in layers) and cholesteric (twisted nematic) phases. Lyotropic liquid crystals are formed by dissolving amphiphilic molecules in a solvent, as in soap-water systems, detergents, DNA and cell membranes.
Applications: Liquid crystals are used in liquid-crystal displays (LCDs) of watches, calculators, computers, televisions and mobile phones, where a small applied voltage reorients the molecules and changes the transmission of light; in thermometers and temperature-sensitive films; in optical shutters and switches; and as stationary phases in gas chromatography.
questions.explanation: The comparison should be made in terms of molecular order: a crystalline solid has both positional and orientational long-range order, a liquid crystal has orientational order with little or no positional order, and an ordinary liquid has neither. The anisotropic optical and electrical properties follow from the partial order and are the basis of the display industry. A good answer names at least one thermotropic and one lyotropic example and distinguishes nematic, smectic and cholesteric phases. Students should note that a liquid crystal is a distinct state of matter, not a mixture of a liquid and a crystal.

questions.question: Quantity of energy released when 1 mole of the ionic crystal is formed from the gaseous ions is called:
