questions.answer: (d) Lattice energy
questions.explanation: Lattice energy is the energy released when one mole of an ionic crystal is formed from its constituent gaseous ions, for example Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → NaCl(s) + 787 kJ mol⁻¹. The oppositely charged ions attract one another strongly, so the process is exothermic and the same quantity of energy is needed to break the lattice apart, which is why lattice energy measures the strength of the ionic bond. Bond energy is the energy required to break a covalent bond, potential energy is energy due to position, and ionization energy is the energy needed to remove an electron from a gaseous atom, so (d) is correct.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Bond energy  (b) Potential energy  (c) Ionization energy  (d) Lattice energy

questions.question: Graphite can conduct electricity in one direction only. With this behavior, it is said to be:
questions.answer: (c) Anisotropic
questions.explanation: A crystal whose physical properties differ when measured along different directions is called anisotropic, and the property itself is anisotropy. In graphite the carbon atoms are joined by strong covalent bonds within each hexagonal layer but the layers are held by weak van der Waals forces; the delocalized electrons move freely only along a layer, so graphite conducts electricity along the layers but hardly at all perpendicular to them. Amorphous solids are isotropic (the same properties in every direction), symmetrical is a geometrical description and not a conductivity property, and polymorphous means that a substance can exist in more than one crystal form, so (c) is correct.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Amorphous  (b) Symmetrical  (c) Anisotropic  (d) Polymorphous

questions.question: NaCl and MgO are isomorphous solids because these have same:
questions.answer: (c) Geometrical shapes
questions.explanation: Isomorphism is the existence of two or more different substances in the same crystalline form: such substances have the same crystal structure, the same geometrical shape of crystal, the same axial ratios and the same coordination of ions. NaCl and MgO both crystallize in the face-centred cubic (rock-salt) structure with 6:6 octahedral coordination, so they are isomorphous because their crystals have the same geometrical shape. Their melting points, boiling points and chemical properties are quite different (MgO is far more refractory and far less soluble), so (a), (b) and (d) cannot be the reason for isomorphism.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Melting point  (b) Boiling point  (c) Geometrical shapes  (d) Chemical Properties

questions.question: The temperature at which two allotropic forms co-exist in equilibrium is called as:
questions.answer: (c) Transition temperature
questions.explanation: The transition temperature is the temperature at which two allotropic (or two crystalline) forms of a substance can exist side by side in equilibrium; at this temperature the two forms have the same free energy, so neither changes into the other. A familiar example is rhombic sulfur ⇌ monoclinic sulfur at 95.6 °C, and another is grey tin ⇌ white tin at 13.2 °C. Melting temperature and fusion temperature are the same thing, namely the temperature at which a solid changes into a liquid, and critical temperature is the temperature above which a gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone, so (c) is correct.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Melting temperature  (b) Fusion temperature  (c) Transition temperature  (d) Critical temperature

questions.question: Diamond is the example of:
questions.answer: (b) Covalent solid
questions.explanation: In diamond every carbon atom is sp³ hybridized and is joined by four strong covalent bonds to four other carbon atoms, so the whole crystal is one continuous three-dimensional covalent network; diamond is therefore a covalent (network) solid. This giant covalent structure makes diamond the hardest natural substance, gives it a very high melting point (about 3550 °C) and makes it a non-conductor because all four valence electrons are used in bonding. Ionic solids are held by electrostatic attraction between ions, metallic solids by a sea of delocalized electrons and molecular solids by weak intermolecular forces, so (b) is correct.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Ionic solid  (b) Covalent solid  (c) Metallic solid  (d) Molecular solid

questions.question: Ice is a molecular solid, the intermolecular force of attraction among its molecules are:
questions.answer: (d) Hydrogen bond
questions.explanation: Ice is a molecular solid built of discrete H₂O molecules. Inside each molecule the O–H bonds are covalent, but the molecules are held together in the crystal by hydrogen bonds, that is the attraction between the partially positive hydrogen atom of one water molecule and the lone pair of the oxygen atom of a neighbouring molecule. Each water molecule can form up to four hydrogen bonds, which gives ice its open, low-density structure, so ice is less dense than liquid water. Ionic, covalent and metallic bonds are strong bonds found inside ionic, covalent network and metallic solids respectively, not between the molecules of a molecular solid, so (d) is correct.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Ionic bond  (b) Covalent bond  (c) Metallic bond  (d) Hydrogen bond

questions.question: If all three axes in unit cell are of different length but all angles are of 90° then it is identified as:
questions.answer: (a) Orthorhombic system
questions.explanation: The orthorhombic system is defined by three crystallographic axes of unequal length (a ≠ b ≠ c) with all three axial angles equal to 90° (α = β = γ = 90°). In the cubic system a = b = c and α = β = γ = 90°; in the tetragonal system a = b ≠ c with all angles 90°; in the hexagonal system a = b ≠ c with α = β = 90° and γ = 120°. Only the orthorhombic system combines unequal axes with right angles, so (a) is correct.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Orthorhombic system  (b) Cubic system  (c) Tetragonal system  (d) Hexagonal system

questions.question: In NaCl, each Na⁺ ion is surrounded by Cl⁻ ions in the numbers:
questions.answer: (c) Six
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride has the face-centred cubic rock-salt structure in which each Na⁺ ion is surrounded octahedrally by six Cl⁻ ions (two along each of the three axes) and each Cl⁻ ion is similarly surrounded by six Na⁺ ions, so the coordination number is 6:6. Three or four would correspond to other structures with lower coordination, and seven is geometrically impossible for this arrangement, so the correct number is six, option (c).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Four  (b) Three  (c) Six  (d) Seven

questions.question: It is an example of crystalline solid:
questions.answer: (a) Alum
questions.explanation: Alum, KAl(SO₄)₂·12H₂O, forms well-defined crystals with flat faces, sharp edges, a definite geometrical shape, a sharp melting point and a regular internal arrangement of ions, so it is a crystalline solid. Glass, plastic and rubber are amorphous: their particles are arranged randomly, they have no long-range order, no sharp melting point and they break with irregular surfaces. Hence alum is the only crystalline solid among the choices, option (a).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Alum  (b) Glass  (c) Plastic  (d) Rubber

questions.question: Each unit cell of sodium chloride consists of:
questions.answer: (c) Four Na⁺ and Four Cl⁻ ions
questions.explanation: In the face-centred cubic unit cell of NaCl the Cl⁻ ions occupy the 8 corners and the 6 face centres, while the Na⁺ ions occupy the 12 edge centres and the 1 body centre. Counting with the share of each position: Cl⁻ = 8 × 1/8 + 6 × 1/2 = 1 + 3 = 4, and Na⁺ = 12 × 1/4 + 1 × 1 = 3 + 1 = 4. The cell therefore contains four Na⁺ and four Cl⁻ ions, that is four formula units of NaCl, which keeps the crystal electrically neutral in the 1:1 ratio. Eight of each ignores the sharing of corner, edge and face ions with neighbouring cells, two of each undercounts the shared positions, and four Na⁺ with six Cl⁻ would not be electrically neutral, so (c) is correct.

options.text: Eight Na⁺ and Eight Cl⁻ ions
Two Na⁺ and Two Cl⁻ ions
Four Na⁺ and Four Cl⁻ ions
Four Na⁺ and Six Cl⁻ ions

questions.optionsRaw: (a) Eight Na⁺ and Eight Cl⁻ ions  (b) Two Na⁺ and Two Cl⁻ ions  (c) Four Na⁺ and Four Cl⁻ ions  (d) Four Na⁺ and Six Cl⁻ ions
questions.correctAnswer: (c) Four Na⁺ and Four Cl⁻ ions

questions.question:
Define the following terms:
(i) Allotropy
(ii) Sublimation
(iii) Melting point
(iv) Unit cell
questions.answer:
(i) Allotropy: Allotropy is the existence of an element in two or more different forms, called allotropes, in the same physical state, the forms differing in the arrangement of the atoms in their crystal lattices and hence in their physical properties. The allotropes contain the same kind of atoms but have different structures, for example carbon exists as diamond, graphite and fullerene, sulfur as rhombic and monoclinic sulfur, and phosphorus as white, red and black phosphorus. The temperature at which two allotropes can co-exist in equilibrium is called the transition temperature.
(ii) Sublimation: Sublimation is the process in which a solid changes directly into its vapour without passing through the liquid state; the reverse process, in which a vapour changes directly into a solid, is called deposition. It takes place when the vapour pressure of the solid becomes equal to the external (atmospheric) pressure at a temperature below its melting point, so the solid passes into vapour from its surface without melting. Iodine, camphor, naphthalene, anthracene and solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) sublime, and the process is used to purify such solids and in freeze drying.
(iii) Melting point: The melting point of a solid is the temperature at which the solid and liquid phases are in equilibrium at one atmosphere pressure, that is the temperature at which the solid changes into a liquid. At this temperature the solid and the liquid co-exist and the heat supplied (the latent heat of fusion) is used to overcome the forces holding the particles in the lattice, so the temperature remains constant until the solid has melted. The melting point is a characteristic property of a pure crystalline solid: ionic and covalent network solids melt at high temperatures, molecular solids at low temperatures, and an impurity lowers and broadens the melting point.
(iv) Unit cell: A unit cell is the smallest repeating portion (the building block) of a crystal lattice which, when translated repeatedly in three dimensions, generates the whole crystal. It is a parallelepiped whose corners are lattice points and which contains the complete structural pattern of the crystal; it is completely described by the lengths of its three edges a, b, c and the three angles α, β, γ between them. A unit cell may be primitive (lattice points only at the corners) or centred (lattice points also at face or body centres).
questions.explanation: These four definitions are the basic vocabulary of the chapter. Allotropy is a structural phenomenon of elements, and the forms are interconvertible at a transition temperature; sublimation is a phase change that bypasses the liquid state and depends on the vapour pressure of the solid reaching atmospheric pressure below the melting point; the melting point is the temperature of solid–liquid equilibrium and is sharp only for pure crystalline solids; and the unit cell is the repeating three-dimensional unit defined by three axial lengths and three axial angles.

questions.question: Define anisotropy. Which type of solids have this property?
questions.answer:
Anisotropy: Anisotropy is the property of a crystal because of which its physical properties, such as refractive index, electrical and thermal conductivity, mechanical strength, cleavage and coefficient of thermal expansion, have different values when measured along different directions in the crystal. It arises because the arrangement of the particles and the distances between them are not the same along different directions in the lattice, so the force holding the particles differs from direction to direction.
Which solids have it: Only crystalline solids show anisotropy. Amorphous solids, in which the particles are arranged randomly, are isotropic, that is they have the same properties in all directions. Examples of anisotropy: graphite conducts electricity along its layers but hardly at all perpendicular to them; mica splits easily along one plane only (perfect cleavage in one direction); the refractive index of quartz is different along and perpendicular to its principal axis; and the mechanical strength of a crystal depends on the direction in which it is stressed.
questions.explanation: Anisotropy is a direct consequence of long-range order: because the lattice is periodic but not the same in every direction, a measured property depends on the direction chosen. Isotropy, its opposite, is shown by amorphous solids and liquids, where the random arrangement makes every direction equivalent. Graphite is the standard example in this chapter, since its electrical conductivity along the layers is many times its conductivity across them.

questions.question: What is Transition temperature? Explain with examples.
questions.answer:
Transition temperature: The temperature at which two different allotropic or crystalline forms of the same substance can exist side by side in equilibrium is called the transition temperature. At this temperature the two forms have the same free energy, so neither form changes into the other; below it the low-temperature form is stable and above it the high-temperature form is stable, and the conversion of one form into the other is a reversible phase transition accompanied by the absorption or evolution of heat.
Examples:
(i) Sulfur: rhombic (α) sulfur changes reversibly into monoclinic (β) sulfur at 95.6 °C. Rhombic sulfur is stable below 95.6 °C and monoclinic sulfur is stable between 95.6 °C and the melting point of sulfur, so 95.6 °C is the transition temperature of sulfur.
(ii) Tin: grey tin (a brittle non-metallic powder) changes into white tin at 13.2 °C. White tin is stable above 13.2 °C, while below this temperature white tin slowly changes into grey tin; this is why tin articles crumble to powder in severe cold, a change known as tin disease or tin pest.
(iii) Potassium nitrate: it changes from the rhombic form into the trigonal form at about 129 °C, which is its transition temperature.
Thus the transition temperature is a characteristic constant of an allotropic substance and it decides which form is stable under a given set of conditions.
questions.explanation: The key idea is equilibrium between two solid forms, not between a solid and its liquid (that is the melting point). Since the two forms have equal free energies at the transition temperature, both can be kept together indefinitely at that temperature. Above and below it only one form is stable, so the physical properties of the substance change abruptly at the transition temperature; the sulfur (95.6 °C) and tin (13.2 °C) examples are the standard illustrations.

questions.question: Explain why diamond is non-conductor of electricity and Graphite is a conductor?
questions.answer:
Diamond is a non-conductor: In diamond every carbon atom is sp³ hybridized and is joined by four strong σ covalent bonds to four other carbon atoms, forming one continuous three-dimensional covalent network. All four valence electrons of each carbon atom are used up in these bonding molecular orbitals, so no free or delocalized electrons are left in the crystal. The filled bonding band is separated from the empty conduction band by a very large energy gap (about 5.5 eV), which electrons cannot cross at ordinary temperature; with no mobile charge carriers, diamond cannot carry an electric current. Diamond is therefore an insulator, although it is an excellent conductor of heat because its rigid lattice transmits vibrations very efficiently.
Graphite is a conductor: In graphite each carbon atom is sp² hybridized and is bonded to only three other carbon atoms, forming flat hexagonal layers. The fourth valence electron of each carbon atom occupies a p orbital perpendicular to the layer, and these p orbitals overlap sideways to give a delocalized π electron cloud above and below each layer. These π electrons are free to move throughout the layer, so when a potential difference is applied they drift in one direction and carry a current. Graphite is therefore a conductor of electricity along its layers, and because the layers are held by weak van der Waals forces, conduction perpendicular to the layers is poor. The same delocalized electrons and weak interlayer forces make graphite soft, black and flaky, in contrast with hard, colourless, insulating diamond, even though both are allotropes of carbon.
questions.explanation: The difference lies entirely in the bonding and in the fate of the fourth valence electron. In diamond all four valence electrons are localized in σ bonds, so there is a filled band separated from an empty band by a large gap. In graphite only three electrons form σ bonds and the fourth is delocalized in a π band that is partly filled, so electrons can move under an applied field. The weak interlayer forces also make graphite's conductivity strongly anisotropic, which links this question to the earlier MCQ on anisotropy.

questions.question: Define lattice energy. Explain how it is effected by size and the charge of ion.
questions.answer:
Lattice energy: The lattice energy of an ionic solid is the energy released when one mole of the solid ionic compound is formed from its constituent gaseous ions, M⁺(g) + X⁻(g) → MX(s). It is also the energy required to separate one mole of the solid into its gaseous ions, so it is a direct measure of the strength of the ionic bond in the crystal. Lattice energy is determined from the Born–Haber cycle and is exothermic when the lattice is formed.
Effect of charge: The electrostatic force between two ions is proportional to the product of their charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, so the lattice energy is approximately proportional to (q₁q₂)/(r₁ + r₂), where q₁ and q₂ are the ionic charges and r₁ + r₂ is the interionic distance. Increasing the charge on either ion increases the attraction sharply and raises the lattice energy: MgO, made of Mg²⁺ and O²⁻, has a lattice energy of about 3900 kJ mol⁻¹ and melts at 2852 °C, whereas NaCl, made of Na⁺ and Cl⁻, has a lattice energy of only about 787 kJ mol⁻¹ and melts at 801 °C.
Effect of size: For ions carrying the same charge, the lattice energy decreases as the ionic radii, and hence the interionic distance, increase, because the centres of charge are then farther apart. Thus the lattice energy and the melting point fall in the order LiF > NaF > KF > RbF > CsF, and MgO (small ions, high charges) is far more stable than BaO (large ions, same charges). Small ions with high charges, such as Al³⁺ and O²⁻ in Al₂O₃, therefore give exceptionally strong lattices with very high lattice energies and melting points.
questions.explanation: Lattice energy measures how strongly the ions are held, so it controls hardness, melting point and solubility. Coulomb's law gives the two trends: lattice energy increases with the product of the charges (doubling each charge quadruples the attraction) and decreases with increasing ionic size (larger separation, weaker attraction). MgO versus NaCl illustrates the charge effect and the alkali-metal halide series illustrates the size effect.

questions.question:
Differentiate between the following:
(i) Crystalline and amorphous solids
(ii) Isomorphism and polymorphism
questions.answer:
(i) Crystalline and amorphous solids:
- Particle arrangement: crystalline solids have a regular, repeating three-dimensional arrangement of particles with long-range order; amorphous solids have a random, disordered arrangement with no long-range order.
- Geometrical shape: crystals have a definite geometrical shape with flat faces, sharp edges and characteristic interfacial angles; amorphous solids have irregular shapes.
- Melting point: crystalline solids have a sharp, definite melting point; amorphous solids soften gradually over a range of temperature.
- Cleavage: crystals split along definite cleavage planes; amorphous solids break irregularly.
- Anisotropy: crystalline solids are anisotropic, their properties differ with direction; amorphous solids are isotropic.
- Examples: crystalline — NaCl, diamond, quartz, sugar, alum; amorphous — glass, rubber, plastic, charcoal.
- Nature: amorphous solids are sometimes described as supercooled liquids or pseudo-solids because their particles are frozen in a disordered arrangement like that of a liquid.
(ii) Isomorphism and polymorphism:
- Definition: isomorphism is the existence of two or more different substances in the same crystalline form; polymorphism is the existence of one and the same substance in more than one crystalline form.
- Number of substances: isomorphism concerns different substances with the same crystal form; polymorphism concerns one substance with different crystal forms.
- Structural requirement: isomorphous substances have the same crystal structure, the same axial ratios and the same coordination; polymorphs differ in the arrangement or coordination of particles in the lattice.
- Examples: isomorphism — NaCl and MgO, K₂SO₄ and K₂CrO₄, ZnSO₄·7H₂O and MgSO₄·7H₂O; polymorphism — rhombic and monoclinic sulfur, calcite and aragonite (CaCO₃), diamond and graphite (the element case is called allotropy).
- Property relation: isomorphous substances usually show analogous chemical formulae and similar chemical behaviour; polymorphs have the same chemical composition but different physical properties such as density, hardness and melting point.
questions.explanation: The two pairs are frequently confused. Crystalline versus amorphous is about the presence or absence of long-range order, which shows up in shape, melting behaviour, cleavage and anisotropy. Isomorphism versus polymorphism is about whether different substances share one crystal form (isomorphism) or one substance takes several crystal forms (polymorphism); allotropy is simply polymorphism shown by an element.

questions.question:
Explain the following with scientific reason.
(i) Why the compressibility of solids is nearly zero?
(ii) Why some solids are sublime in nature?
questions.answer:
(i) The compressibility of solids is nearly zero because in a solid the constituent particles (ions, atoms or molecules) are packed very closely together and are held in their positions by strong forces, namely ionic, covalent or metallic bonds or strong intermolecular forces. There is therefore very little empty space between the particles. When pressure is applied the particles cannot be pushed appreciably closer, because the repulsion between their electron clouds rises steeply as they are forced together; the solid resists compression and has a very high bulk modulus. A solid can be deformed only slightly, and its volume changes by a very small fraction unless the solid is actually broken, which is why solids are described as rigid and incompressible.
(ii) Some solids sublime because their molecules are held in the crystal by weak intermolecular forces, such as van der Waals forces, dipole–dipole attractions or hydrogen bonds, while the atoms inside each molecule are joined by strong covalent bonds. Such molecular solids have a low enthalpy of sublimation and a relatively high vapour pressure at temperatures below their melting point. When this vapour pressure becomes equal to the atmospheric pressure, the molecules escape directly from the surface of the solid as vapour and the solid sublimes without melting. Non-polar molecular solids with nearly spherical molecules behave in this way: iodine, naphthalene, anthracene, camphor and solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) all sublime, and the process is used to purify such solids.
questions.explanation: Both answers come from the same picture of a solid: close packing with strong forces gives rigidity and very low compressibility, whereas weak intermolecular forces inside a molecular lattice allow molecules to escape into the vapour phase without the lattice melting. Sublimation is favoured when the solid's vapour pressure reaches atmospheric pressure below its melting point, which is typical of molecular solids with weak intermolecular attractions.

questions.question: Define unit cell. Draw a diagram to show its axial distances and axial angles.
questions.answer:
Definition: A unit cell is the smallest repeating unit of a crystal lattice, the smallest portion of the crystal which, when translated repeatedly in three dimensions, builds up the entire crystal. It is a parallelepiped whose corners are occupied by lattice points and which contains the complete structural pattern of the crystal; the whole crystal is obtained by stacking identical unit cells side by side in the three directions. A unit cell is described by six parameters: the three axial lengths a, b and c and the three axial angles α, β and γ.
Diagram (described in words): Draw a parallelepiped, that is a box-like figure which is oblique in the general case and whose eight corners are lattice points. Take the lower-front-left corner as the origin O and draw the three edges that meet there: O→A of length a along the x-direction, O→B of length b along the y-direction, and O→C of length c along the z-direction. Label these three axial distances a, b and c on the three edges. Mark the three axial angles at O inside the cell: α is the angle between the edges b and c (between OB and OC), β is the angle between the edges a and c (between OA and OC), and γ is the angle between the edges a and b (between OA and OB). Thus a, b and c are the axial distances and α, β and γ are the axial angles. For a simple cubic unit cell a = b = c and α = β = γ = 90°, so the six faces are squares and the three edges are mutually perpendicular; in the general triclinic cell a ≠ b ≠ c and α ≠ β ≠ γ ≠ 90°. The seven crystal systems are classified by these six parameters: cubic (a = b = c, α = β = γ = 90°), tetragonal (a = b ≠ c, all angles 90°), orthorhombic (a ≠ b ≠ c, all angles 90°), hexagonal (a = b ≠ c, α = β = 90°, γ = 120°), rhombohedral (a = b = c, α = β = γ ≠ 90°), monoclinic (a ≠ b ≠ c, two angles 90°) and triclinic (a ≠ b ≠ c, no angle 90°).
questions.explanation: The unit cell is the geometrical basis of crystal description: its three edge lengths and three interfacial angles are the six lattice parameters, and their values sort every crystal into one of the seven systems. Note carefully the conventional pairing of the angles with the edges: α lies between b and c, β between a and c, and γ between a and b, all measured at a common corner of the cell.

questions.question: Give four properties of ionic solids. How can you determine the number of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in a unit cell of sodium chloride?
questions.answer:
Four properties of ionic solids:
(i) Hard and brittle: the ions are held by strong electrostatic forces in a rigid lattice, so ionic solids are hard; when a blow is struck the layers of ions are displaced so that ions of like charge come opposite one another, and the resulting repulsion makes the crystal break, so it is brittle.
(ii) High melting and boiling points: a large amount of energy is needed to overcome the strong electrostatic attraction between the ions, for example NaCl melts at 801 °C and MgO melts at 2852 °C.
(iii) Non-conductors in the solid state but conductors when molten or in aqueous solution: in the solid the ions are held in fixed positions and cannot move, but on melting or on dissolving in water the ions become free to move and the liquid conducts electricity; this conduction is electrolytic and is accompanied by chemical change at the electrodes.
(iv) Soluble in polar solvents such as water and insoluble in non-polar solvents such as benzene and carbon tetrachloride: the polar water molecules attract and surround the ions, pulling them out of the lattice and hydrating them. Ionic solids are also crystalline and have high lattice energies.
Number of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in the unit cell of sodium chloride: NaCl crystallizes in the face-centred cubic (rock-salt) structure, and the number of ions is found by counting the ions at each type of position and multiplying by the fraction of each ion that lies inside the cell.
- Cl⁻ ions: 8 at the corners, each shared by 8 adjacent cells, give 8 × 1/8 = 1; 6 at the face centres, each shared by 2 cells, give 6 × 1/2 = 3. Total Cl⁻ = 1 + 3 = 4.
- Na⁺ ions: 12 at the edge centres, each shared by 4 cells, give 12 × 1/4 = 3; 1 at the body centre, wholly inside the cell, gives 1 × 1 = 1. Total Na⁺ = 3 + 1 = 4.
Hence one unit cell contains 4 Na⁺ and 4 Cl⁻ ions, that is 4 formula units of NaCl, which agrees with the 1:1 ratio needed for electrical neutrality and gives the formula NaCl.
questions.explanation: The counting method depends on the fraction of each ion that belongs to a given cell: a corner ion is shared by eight cells, an edge-centre ion by four, a face-centre ion by two and a body-centre ion belongs entirely to one cell. Applying these fractions to the rock-salt structure gives 4 Cl⁻ and 4 Na⁺ per unit cell, i.e. four NaCl formula units.

questions.question: Give a brief account on metallic solids. Why they conduct heat and electricity?
questions.answer:
Metallic solids: Metallic solids are crystalline solids in which the atoms of a metal are packed closely together and the lattice consists of positive metal ions (kernels) surrounded by a sea of delocalized valence electrons that belong to the crystal as a whole rather than to any single atom. The attraction between the positive ions and this mobile electron cloud is the metallic bond; it is non-directional, so the metal ions behave as spheres of equal size packed in a close arrangement such as face-centred cubic, body-centred cubic or hexagonal close packing. Examples are all metals and alloys: copper, iron, aluminium, silver, gold and sodium, with mercury being the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.
Properties: metallic lustre, because the free electrons absorb and re-emit light of all wavelengths; high electrical and thermal conductivity; malleability and ductility, because layers of ions can slide over one another without breaking the non-directional metallic bond; generally high melting and boiling points (except mercury and the soft alkali metals); and they are opaque, dense and crystalline.
Why they conduct electricity: the delocalized electrons are free to move throughout the crystal. When a potential difference is applied across the metal the electrons drift in one direction and carry charge from one end to the other, so the metal conducts. This conduction is electronic and does not involve any chemical change, unlike the electrolytic conduction of ionic solids.
Why they conduct heat: the free electrons at the hot end gain kinetic energy and move rapidly through the lattice, colliding with other electrons and with the metal ions and transferring energy to them; the vibrations of the ions also help to carry energy, but the electrons are far more effective, which is why metals conduct heat much better than non-metals.
questions.explanation: The electron-sea model explains all the characteristic properties of metals: mobility of the delocalized electrons gives electrical and thermal conductivity, their interaction with light gives metallic lustre, and the non-directional nature of the metallic bond allows the layers of ions to slide, giving malleability and ductility. Because the carriers are electrons and not ions, metallic conduction produces no chemical change.

questions.question: What is meant by polymorphism? How it is related to allotropy. Give your answer with examples.
questions.answer:
Polymorphism: Polymorphism is the existence of one and the same substance in more than one crystalline form, the different forms being called polymorphs. The forms differ in the arrangement or coordination of the particles in the crystal lattice, so they differ in physical properties such as density, hardness, melting point, solubility and refractive index, although the chemical composition is the same in all of them. The forms are interconvertible at a definite temperature, the transition temperature, and the form that is stable depends on the temperature and pressure.
Relation to allotropy: When the substance that shows polymorphism is an element, the phenomenon is called allotropy and the forms are called allotropes. Allotropy is therefore a special case of polymorphism: all allotropes are polymorphs, but not all polymorphs are allotropes, because the term allotropy is reserved for elements. Some books use polymorphism for compounds and allotropy for elements, but the underlying phenomenon, the existence of more than one crystal form of the same substance, is identical in both cases.
Examples:
(i) Carbon (allotropy): diamond, in which each carbon atom is sp³ hybridized and bonded to four others in a three-dimensional network, and graphite, in which each carbon atom is sp² hybridized and forms hexagonal layers, and fullerene, C₆₀, a molecular allotrope.
(ii) Sulfur (allotropy): rhombic (α) sulfur, stable below 95.6 °C, and monoclinic (β) sulfur, stable above 95.6 °C, with a transition temperature of 95.6 °C.
(iii) Phosphorus (allotropy): white, red and black phosphorus.
(iv) Compounds (polymorphism): calcium carbonate as calcite and aragonite, calcium sulfate as gypsum and anhydrite, and silica as quartz, tridymite and cristobalite.
questions.explanation: The distinction is one of scope rather than of mechanism: polymorphism is the general term for a substance crystallizing in more than one form, and allotropy is the same behaviour shown by an element. The polymorphs differ in lattice arrangement, so their physical properties differ even though their chemical composition is identical, and the temperature at which one form changes into the other is the transition temperature.

questions.question: Molecular solids are soft and possess low melting point, how can you justify this statement?
questions.answer:
Justification: In a molecular solid the lattice is built of discrete molecules, for example H₂O, I₂, CO₂, naphthalene and sugar. Within each molecule the atoms are held by strong covalent bonds, but the molecules themselves are held together by weak intermolecular forces, namely London dispersion forces, dipole–dipole attractions and, in some cases, hydrogen bonds. These intermolecular forces are much weaker than ionic, covalent or metallic bonds: they typically amount to only a few to a few tens of kJ mol⁻¹, whereas a covalent bond is of the order of hundreds of kJ mol⁻¹.
Why they are soft: when a molecular solid is pressed, scratched or deformed, only the weak intermolecular forces have to be overcome, and whole molecules slide over one another easily. Molecular solids are therefore soft, waxy, easily broken or powdered, as seen in iodine, naphthalene, wax and sugar crystals.
Why they have low melting points: melting and boiling require only the separation of the molecules from one another, not the breaking of the covalent bonds inside the molecules. The small amount of energy needed to overcome the weak intermolecular forces is supplied at a low temperature, so molecular solids melt and boil at low temperatures. For example ice melts at 0 °C, naphthalene at 80 °C and iodine at 114 °C, while solid CO₂ sublimes at −78.5 °C; in contrast, the covalent network solid diamond melts at about 3550 °C and the ionic solid NaCl at 801 °C.
Other consequences of the weak intermolecular forces: molecular solids are poor conductors of electricity in the solid, molten or dissolved state because they contain no free ions or electrons; they are volatile and many sublime readily; and they are usually soluble in non-polar solvents. Hydrogen bonding in ice raises its melting point above that of other small molecular solids and gives ice an open structure, which is why ice is less dense than water, but even then its melting point is low compared with those of ionic and covalent network solids.
questions.explanation: The statement is justified by the difference between the strong covalent bonds inside a molecule and the weak intermolecular forces between molecules. Since melting and softening only require the molecules to move apart, the energy needed is small, so molecular solids are soft and melt at low temperatures; the same weak forces make them volatile, non-conducting and soluble in non-polar solvents.

questions.question: In the equilibrium system of PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g), the correct relationship between Kc and Kp is:
questions.answer: (a) Kp > Kc
questions.explanation: Kp and Kc are related by Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants. For PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g), Δn = (1 + 1) − 1 = +1, so Kp = Kc(RT)¹ = KcRT. Since RT is greater than 1 at ordinary temperatures (at 298 K, RT = 0.0821 × 298 = 24.5 dm³ atm mol⁻¹), Kp is greater than Kc, that is Kp > Kc. Option (b) would be true only if Δn were negative, option (c) only if Δn = 0, and option (d), Kp/Kc = 1, is simply another way of writing Kp = Kc, so (a) is correct.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Kp > Kc  (b) Kp < Kc  (c) Kp = Kc  (d) Kp/Kc = 1

questions.question: The equilibrium of which of the following reaction would not be affected by an increase in pressure:
questions.answer: (c) N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)
questions.explanation: A change in pressure shifts an equilibrium only when the number of gaseous moles changes, because the system then responds by moving towards the side having fewer gas molecules. For N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g), Δn = 2 − (1 + 1) = 0; the number of gaseous moles is the same on both sides, so compression raises all partial pressures in the same proportion and leaves the equilibrium position unchanged. In (a) Δn = +1, so an increase in pressure shifts the equilibrium to the left (towards PCl₅); in (b) Δn = 2 − 3 = −1 and in (d) Δn = 2 − 3 = −1, so an increase in pressure shifts both of them to the right. Hence only (c) is unaffected, and (c) is correct.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g)  (b) 2NO(g) + Cl₂(g) ⇌ 2NOCl(g)  (c) N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)  (d) 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g)

questions.question: What happens to the value of Kc when a catalyst is added to a chemical system at equilibrium?
questions.answer: (d) It remains unchanged
questions.explanation: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway of lower activation energy and lowers the activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions by exactly the same amount. Both rates are therefore increased by the same factor, so the ratio kf/kr, which is equal to Kc, does not change; the catalyst merely shortens the time required to reach equilibrium. The equilibrium position, the equilibrium concentrations and the value of Kc all remain unchanged, so (d) is correct. Kc changes only when the temperature is changed, so (a), (b) and (c) are wrong.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) It decreases  (b) It increases  (c) It becomes zero  (d) It remains unchanged

questions.question: The correct Ksp expression of a sparingly soluble salt Li₂C₂O₄ among the following is:
questions.answer: (b) Ksp = [Li⁺]²[C₂O₄²⁻]
questions.explanation: Lithium oxalate dissolves as Li₂C₂O₄(s) ⇌ 2Li⁺(aq) + C₂O₄²⁻(aq). The solubility product is the product of the molar concentrations of the ions in the saturated solution, each raised to the power equal to its coefficient in the balanced equation, so Ksp = [Li⁺]²[C₂O₄²⁻]. Option (a) omits the square on [Li⁺]; options (c) and (d) wrongly place the stoichiometric coefficient 2 inside the concentration term, writing [2Li⁺], instead of using it as an exponent. Hence (b) is correct.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Ksp = [Li⁺][C₂O₄²⁻]  (b) Ksp = [Li⁺]²[C₂O₄²⁻]  (c) Ksp = [2Li⁺][C₂O₄²⁻]  (d) Ksp = [2Li⁺]²[C₂O₄²⁻]²

questions.question: If the equilibrium expression of a reversible reaction is Kc = [C]²/([A][B]), the balanced equilibrium equation should be:
questions.answer: (d) A + B ⇌ 2C
questions.explanation: In the expression Kc = [C]²/([A][B]), the product concentrations appear in the numerator and the reactant concentrations in the denominator, each raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient. The squared term [C]² means that two moles of C are formed, while [A] and [B] each appear to the first power, so one mole of A reacts with one mole of B. The balanced equation is therefore A + B ⇌ 2C. Option (a) would give Kc = [A][B]/[C], option (b) would give Kc = [C]/([A][B]) and option (c) would give Kc = [A][B]/[C]², so (d) is correct.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) C ⇌ A + B  (b) A + B ⇌ C  (c) 2C ⇌ A + B  (d) A + B ⇌ 2C

questions.question: The equilibrium of N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g) (ΔH = +ve) is affected by change in:
questions.answer: (a) Temperature only
questions.explanation: For N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g), Δn = 2 − (1 + 1) = 0, so a change in pressure does not shift this equilibrium and has no effect on it. The forward reaction is endothermic (ΔH = +ve), so raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the forward direction and increases the value of Kc, while lowering the temperature shifts it backwards. Temperature is therefore the only variable among the choices that affects this equilibrium, so (a) is correct and (b), (c), (d) are wrong.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Temperature only  (b) Pressure only  (c) Both temperature and pressure  (d) Neither temperature nor pressure

questions.question: In the reaction A(g) + B(g) ⇌ 2C(g), the equilibrium constants Kp = Kc because:
questions.answer: (d) Δn = 0
questions.explanation: The two equilibrium constants are related by Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn is the change in the number of moles of gas: Δn = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants. For A(g) + B(g) ⇌ 2C(g), Δn = 2 − (1 + 1) = 0, so (RT)^Δn = (RT)⁰ = 1 and therefore Kp = Kc. The condition required is Δn = 0, not Δn = 1, so (d) is correct while (a), (b) and (c) are wrong.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Δn > 1  (b) Δn < 1  (c) Δn = 1  (d) Δn = 0

questions.question: The term active mass use in law of mass action means:
questions.answer: (c) mole per dm³
questions.explanation: Active mass means the molar concentration of a substance, that is the number of moles of the substance per cubic decimetre of the solution or of the gaseous mixture: active mass = n/V, expressed in mol dm⁻³. The law of mass action is stated in terms of these molar concentrations, so mole per dm³ is the correct meaning and (c) is correct. The number of moles alone does not define a concentration because it ignores the volume, the number of molecules is not a concentration, and gram per dm³ is a mass concentration rather than a molar concentration.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) No. of mole  (b) No. of molecules  (c) mole per dm³  (d) gram per dm³

questions.question: NaCl when added to an aqueous silver chloride solution:
questions.answer: (a) Decreases the solubility of AgCl
questions.explanation: Silver chloride is sparingly soluble and dissolves as AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq). Adding NaCl introduces the common ion Cl⁻, so the ionic product [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] immediately exceeds Ksp and, by Le Chatelier's principle, the equilibrium shifts to the left, precipitating more AgCl and lowering [Ag⁺]. The solubility of AgCl therefore decreases; this is the common ion effect. Hence (a) is correct. Option (d), printed as does not effect, is wrong because the added Cl⁻ does affect the solubility, and (b) and (c) are also wrong.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Decreases the solubility of AgCl  (b) Increases the solubility of AgCl  (c) Forms a clear solution  (d) Does not effect

questions.question: Some reactions are nearly to completion in the forward direction and identified by their:
questions.answer: (a) Very high value of Kc
questions.explanation: For a reaction that goes nearly to completion in the forward direction, the equilibrium mixture contains mainly products and very little reactant, so the ratio of the product of product concentrations to the product of reactant concentrations is very large and Kc is very large (Kc >> 1). The magnitude of Kc measures the extent of reaction: a very low Kc means the reaction hardly proceeds in the forward direction. The enthalpy change ΔH tells how much heat is evolved or absorbed but not how far the reaction goes, so (a) is correct.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Very high value of Kc  (b) Very low value of Kc  (c) Very high value of ΔH  (d) Very low value of ΔH

questions.question:
Define the following:
(i) Reversible reaction
(ii) Chemical equilibrium
questions.answer:
(i) Reversible reaction: A reversible reaction is a chemical reaction in which the products formed can react together, under the same conditions, to give back the original reactants, so the change proceeds in both the forward and the reverse directions. It is written with a double arrow (⇌) and never goes to completion; it ends in a state of equilibrium in which both reactants and products are present. The reaction can be started from either the reactants or the products side, and at a given temperature the same equilibrium constant is established, although the final amounts depend on the initial amounts, temperature and pressure. Examples: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g); PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g); H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g); CH₃COOH(l) + C₂H₅OH(l) ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅(l) + H₂O(l). In an irreversible reaction, written with a single arrow (→), such as AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq), the reverse reaction is negligible and the reaction goes to completion.
(ii) Chemical equilibrium: Chemical equilibrium is the state of a reversible reaction in which the rate of the forward reaction becomes equal to the rate of the reverse reaction, so that the concentrations of the reactants and products remain constant with time. It is dynamic in nature: both reactions continue at the molecular level, but they proceed at equal rates, so no net change is observed. At equilibrium the free energy of the system is minimum, and the ratio of the product of the concentrations of the products to the product of the concentrations of the reactants, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient, is constant at a given temperature; this constant is the equilibrium constant Kc. Equilibrium can be attained from either the reactants or the products side, and a catalyst does not change the equilibrium position but only speeds up its attainment. The equilibrium position shifts when temperature, pressure or concentration is changed. Examples: the physical equilibrium H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂O(g) in a closed vessel, and the chemical equilibrium H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g).
questions.explanation: Both definitions depend on the two opposing rates becoming equal. A reversible reaction is recognized by the double arrow and by the fact that it does not go to completion, whereas an irreversible reaction has a single arrow and goes to completion. Chemical equilibrium is a dynamic state, not a stopped reaction: the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, which is why the concentrations stay constant while both reactants and products remain present. The equilibrium constant Kc expresses the fixed ratio of concentrations at a given temperature.

questions.question:
Write expression of Kc and Kp for the following reversible reactions.
(i) 2NO₂(g) + 7H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) + 4H₂O(g)
(ii) 2H₂S(g) + 3O₂(g) ⇌ 2H₂O(g) + 2SO₂(g)
questions.answer:
(i) 2NO₂(g) + 7H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) + 4H₂O(g)
Kc = [NH₃]²[H₂O]⁴/([NO₂]²[H₂]⁷)
Kp = (pNH₃)²(pH₂O)⁴/[(pNO₂)²(pH₂)⁷]
Here Δn = (2 + 4) − (2 + 7) = 6 − 9 = −3, so Kp = Kc(RT)⁻³. Because Δn is negative, Kc has the unit (mol dm⁻³)⁻³ = dm⁹ mol⁻³, and Kp has the unit atm⁻³ when the partial pressures are expressed in atmospheres.
(ii) 2H₂S(g) + 3O₂(g) ⇌ 2H₂O(g) + 2SO₂(g)
Kc = [H₂O]²[SO₂]²/([H₂S]²[O₂]³)
Kp = (pH₂O)²(pSO₂)²/[(pH₂S)²(pO₂)³]
Here Δn = (2 + 2) − (2 + 3) = 4 − 5 = −1, so Kp = Kc(RT)⁻¹. Because Δn is negative, Kc has the unit (mol dm⁻³)⁻¹ = dm³ mol⁻¹, and Kp has the unit atm⁻¹ when the partial pressures are expressed in atmospheres.
questions.explanation: In Kc the concentration of each gaseous product is placed in the numerator and that of each gaseous reactant in the denominator, each raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation. Kp is written in the same way with partial pressures in place of molar concentrations, and the two are connected by Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants. For (i) Δn = −3 and for (ii) Δn = −1; the units of Kc follow from (mol dm⁻³)^Δn, and those of Kp from (atm)^Δn. Pure solids and liquids are omitted from both expressions.

questions.question:
(a) Define solubility product.
(b) Write the solubility product expression of the following salts: BaF₂, Li₂C₂O₄, MgCO₃, Ag₃PO₄
questions.answer:
(a) Solubility product: The solubility product of a sparingly soluble salt is the product of the molar concentrations of its constituent ions in a saturated solution at equilibrium with the undissolved solid, each concentration being raised to the power equal to the number of ions of that kind furnished by one formula unit of the salt. For a salt that gives x cations Mʸ⁺ and y anions Xˣ⁻ per formula unit, the solubility product is Ksp = [Mʸ⁺]ˣ[Xˣ⁻]ʸ. It is an equilibrium constant for the dissolution equilibrium, so it depends only on temperature and not on the amounts of solid or on the separate concentrations of the ions. Comparing the ionic product Q of a solution with Ksp predicts precipitation: if Q < Ksp the solution is unsaturated and no precipitate forms, if Q = Ksp it is just saturated, and if Q > Ksp it is supersaturated and the salt precipitates until Q falls to Ksp.
(b) Solubility product expressions:
- BaF₂: BaF₂(s) ⇌ Ba²⁺(aq) + 2F⁻(aq); Ksp = [Ba²⁺][F⁻]² (unit mol³ dm⁻⁹).
- Li₂C₂O₄: Li₂C₂O₄(s) ⇌ 2Li⁺(aq) + C₂O₄²⁻(aq); Ksp = [Li⁺]²[C₂O₄²⁻] (unit mol³ dm⁻⁹).
- MgCO₃: MgCO₃(s) ⇌ Mg²⁺(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq); Ksp = [Mg²⁺][CO₃²⁻] (unit mol² dm⁻⁶).
- Ag₃PO₄: Ag₃PO₄(s) ⇌ 3Ag⁺(aq) + PO₄³⁻(aq); Ksp = [Ag⁺]³[PO₄³⁻] (unit mol⁴ dm⁻¹²).
questions.explanation: The exponents in a Ksp expression are the numbers of ions produced by one formula unit, never the coefficients written inside the brackets. Thus BaF₂ gives one Ba²⁺ and two F⁻, so [F⁻] is squared; Li₂C₂O₄ gives two Li⁺ and one C₂O₄²⁻, so [Li⁺] is squared; MgCO₃ gives one ion of each kind, so both are to the first power; and Ag₃PO₄ gives three Ag⁺ and one PO₄³⁻, so [Ag⁺] is cubed. The pure solid does not appear in the expression because its concentration is constant. The units are (mol dm⁻³) raised to the total number of ions produced by one formula unit: 3 ions for BaF₂ and Li₂C₂O₄ (mol³ dm⁻⁹), 2 ions for MgCO₃ (mol² dm⁻⁶), and 4 ions for Ag₃PO₄ (mol⁴ dm⁻¹²).

questions.question:
Using Le-Chatelier's principle, explain three ways in which yield of SO₃ can be increase in Contact process.
2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g)    (ΔH° = −ve)
questions.answer:
Le Chatelier's principle states that if a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in temperature, pressure or concentration of one of its components, the system shifts its equilibrium position in the direction that tends to oppose the disturbance. For the Contact process, 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH° = −ve (exothermic) and Δn = 2 − 3 = −1.
(i) By lowering the temperature: the forward reaction is exothermic, so removing heat shifts the equilibrium to the right and increases the yield of SO₃. In practice the temperature is kept at about 400–450 °C rather than very low, because at low temperature the rate of reaction becomes too slow even in the presence of the catalyst.
(ii) By increasing the pressure: the forward direction produces fewer moles of gas (3 moles of reactants give 2 moles of SO₃), so an increase in pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right and increases the yield of SO₃. A pressure of about 2 atm (in some plants up to 10 atm) is used, since very high pressure requires expensive equipment.
(iii) By removing SO₃ as it is formed or by using an excess of a reactant: continuous removal of SO₃, for example by absorbing it in concentrated H₂SO₄, keeps its concentration low and the equilibrium shifts continuously to the right. Alternatively, passing an excess of air (oxygen) increases the concentration of O₂, which also shifts the equilibrium to the right and raises the yield of SO₃. The V₂O₅ catalyst is used to attain equilibrium rapidly, but being a catalyst it does not change the equilibrium yield.
questions.explanation: The direction of the shift is decided by two features of the balanced equation: ΔH° is negative, so the forward reaction is exothermic and low temperature favours the products; Δn is negative, so the forward reaction produces fewer gas molecules and high pressure favours the products. The third way changes the concentration term: removing SO₃ or adding excess O₂ makes the reaction quotient smaller than Kc, so the reaction must move forward to restore equilibrium. Temperature and pressure changes alter Kc or the partial pressures, while concentration changes leave Kc unchanged but shift the position of equilibrium. The industrial conditions of about 400–450 °C, 2 atm and a V₂O₅ catalyst are a compromise between maximum yield and an acceptable rate.

questions.question: State Law of mass action and derive Kc expression of a general reversible reaction.
questions.answer:
Law of mass action: The law of mass action, proposed by Guldberg and Waage in 1864, states that the rate of a chemical reaction is directly proportional to the product of the active masses (molar concentrations) of the reactants, each raised to the power equal to its stoichiometric coefficient in the balanced chemical equation. For a general reversible reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, the rate of the forward reaction is proportional to [A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ and the rate of the reverse reaction is proportional to [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ.
Derivation of Kc: Let kf and kr be the rate constants of the forward and reverse reactions.
Forward rate: Rf = kf[A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ
Reverse rate: Rr = kr[C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ
At equilibrium the two rates become equal, so Rf = Rr:
kf[A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ = kr[C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ
Rearranging, [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ/([A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ) = kf/kr
Since kf and kr are constants at a given temperature, their ratio is also a constant. This constant is called the equilibrium constant Kc:
Kc = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ/([A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ)
Thus for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), Kc = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]); for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), Kc = [NH₃]²/([N₂][H₂]³). The concentrations in the expression are the equilibrium molar concentrations in mol dm⁻³, and pure solids and pure liquids are omitted because their concentrations are constant. Kc depends only on temperature and is independent of the initial concentrations, the pressure and the presence of a catalyst. For gaseous reactions it is related to Kp by Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn.
questions.explanation: The derivation uses the fact that equilibrium is dynamic: the forward and reverse reactions continue but at equal rates. Setting the two rate laws equal and dividing both sides by the reverse rate constant and by [A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ isolates the ratio kf/kr, which is constant at constant temperature and is defined as Kc. The exponents come from the stoichiometric coefficients of the balanced equation, so the expression must be written only after the equation has been balanced. Because Kc is a ratio of rate constants, it is unchanged by catalysts (which change kf and kr equally) and by pressure or initial amounts, but it changes with temperature.

questions.question: State Le-Chatelier's principle. Explain the industrial application of Le-Chatelier's principle using Haber's process.
questions.answer:
Le Chatelier's principle: If a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in temperature, pressure or concentration of one of its components, the system shifts its equilibrium position in the direction that tends to oppose or minimize the effect of the change. In other words, the system adjusts itself so as to absorb the disturbance: adding a reactant shifts the equilibrium forward, increasing the pressure shifts it towards the side with fewer gas molecules, and raising the temperature shifts it in the endothermic direction.
Application to Haber's process: Ammonia is manufactured by the reversible reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92.4 kJ mol⁻¹, Δn = 2 − 4 = −2. The forward reaction is exothermic and is accompanied by a decrease in the number of gas molecules, so Le Chatelier's principle predicts that low temperature and high pressure favour the formation of ammonia.
(i) Effect of pressure: since four moles of gaseous reactants give two moles of ammonia, an increase in pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right and increases the yield. Industrially a pressure of about 200 atm (150–300 atm) is used.
(ii) Effect of temperature: the forward reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature increases the equilibrium yield. However, at low temperature the rate of reaction is extremely slow, so a compromise temperature of about 450–500 °C is employed together with a catalyst.
(iii) Effect of concentration: ammonia is removed continuously by liquefying it (cooling the gaseous mixture), which keeps the concentration of NH₃ low and drives the equilibrium forward; unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled, and an excess of the reactants is maintained.
(iv) Effect of catalyst: finely divided iron with promoters such as K₂O and Al₂O₃ is used. The catalyst does not change the equilibrium position or the yield; it only enables equilibrium to be reached rapidly at the moderate temperature used. Under these conditions the yield is about 15–20% per pass, and recycling of the unreacted gases makes the overall conversion high.
questions.explanation: The Haber process is the standard industrial illustration of Le Chatelier's principle because thermodynamics and kinetics pull in different directions: the exothermic forward reaction gives a higher equilibrium yield at low temperature, but the rate then becomes impractically slow. High pressure is favourable both thermodynamically (fewer gas molecules) and kinetically, so about 200 atm is used. The compromise temperature of 450–500 °C with an iron catalyst balances yield against speed. Removing NH₃ as it is formed lowers the reaction quotient below Kc, so the reaction continues to move forward, and recycling the unreacted gases raises the overall efficiency.

questions.question: Give brief account on Common ion effect.
questions.answer:
Common ion effect: The common ion effect is the suppression of the ionization or of the solubility of a weak electrolyte or a sparingly soluble salt by the addition of a strong electrolyte that furnishes one of the same ions. The added ion is called the common ion, and its presence shifts the equilibrium of the weak electrolyte backwards, decreasing the degree of ionization or the solubility.
Explanation by Le Chatelier's principle: Consider a weak acid such as acetic acid, CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺. If sodium acetate, CH₃COONa, is added, it dissociates completely to give CH₃COO⁻, so the concentration of the common ion CH₃COO⁻ increases. According to Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts to the left, more CH₃COOH is formed, the concentration of H⁺ falls and the degree of ionization of the acid decreases.
Example with a sparingly soluble salt: Silver chloride dissolves as AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq). Adding NaCl increases [Cl⁻], so the ionic product [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] exceeds Ksp and the equilibrium shifts to the left, precipitating more AgCl; the solubility of AgCl is therefore lower in sodium chloride solution than in pure water. Similarly, the solubility of CaCO₃ decreases when Na₂CO₃ is added, and the solubility of BaSO₄ decreases in the presence of Na₂SO₄.
Applications: The common ion effect is used in qualitative and quantitative analysis, for example to precipitate a cation completely as its sparingly soluble salt by adding an excess of the precipitating reagent; to separate ions of different groups; in gravimetric analysis, where it reduces the solubility loss of the precipitate; in the preparation of buffer solutions, where a mixture of a weak acid and its salt controls the pH; and in salting out, where adding a salt with a common ion decreases the solubility of a substance and helps it to separate.
questions.explanation: The effect is a direct consequence of the equilibrium law: adding an ion that already appears in the equilibrium expression increases the value of the reaction quotient, so the system shifts in the direction that consumes that ion. For a weak electrolyte this lowers the degree of ionization; for a sparingly soluble salt it lowers the solubility by making the ionic product exceed Ksp. The effect is strongest when the added common ion is in large excess, and it explains why precipitates are washed with a dilute solution of a salt containing the common ion rather than with pure water.

questions.question:
Define equilibrium constant (Kc). How it helps in predicting the
(i) Direction of reaction
(ii) Extent of reaction.
questions.answer:
Equilibrium constant (Kc): For a reversible reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, the equilibrium constant Kc is the ratio of the product of the equilibrium molar concentrations of the products to the product of the equilibrium molar concentrations of the reactants, each concentration raised to the power equal to its stoichiometric coefficient:
Kc = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ/([A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ)
It is a constant at a given temperature, equals the ratio kf/kr, and does not depend on the initial concentrations, on pressure or on the presence of a catalyst. Pure solids and liquids are not included, and for gaseous reactions Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn.
(i) Direction of reaction: The direction in which a reaction mixture will proceed is found by calculating the reaction quotient Qc from the concentrations at that instant, using the same expression as Kc but with the actual (not necessarily equilibrium) concentrations. Then:
- If Qc < Kc, the ratio of products to reactants is too small, so the reaction proceeds in the forward direction until Qc becomes equal to Kc.
- If Qc > Kc, the ratio is too large, so the reaction proceeds in the reverse direction.
- If Qc = Kc, the system is already at equilibrium and no net change occurs.
For example, if for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI (Kc = 49) a mixture has Qc = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]) = 4, then Qc < Kc and the reaction goes forward, producing more HI.
(ii) Extent of reaction: The magnitude of Kc shows how far the reaction proceeds before reaching equilibrium. A very large Kc (Kc >> 1, for example of the order of 10³³ for the formation of HCl at 25 °C) means that the products strongly predominate and the reaction is nearly complete in the forward direction. A very small Kc (Kc << 1, for example about 10⁻³⁰ for N₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2NO at room temperature) means that very little product is formed and the reaction hardly proceeds forward. An intermediate value of Kc (of the order of 1 to 10²) means that appreciable amounts of both reactants and products are present at equilibrium. The extent is also related to the standard free energy change by ΔG° = −RT ln Kc: a negative ΔG° corresponds to Kc > 1 and a reaction that proceeds forward, while a positive ΔG° corresponds to Kc < 1.
questions.explanation: The reaction quotient Qc and the equilibrium constant Kc have identical mathematical forms; the only difference is that Qc uses the instantaneous concentrations while Kc uses the equilibrium concentrations. Comparing them tells the direction of the shift, and after the shift Qc becomes equal to Kc. The size of Kc, on the other hand, is fixed by temperature and tells the position of equilibrium, that is the extent of the reaction, not its speed; a large Kc does not mean a fast reaction, and a catalyst changes the rate but not Kc.

questions.question:
At 444°C reaction of hydrogen and iodine is performed in a sealed 1 dm³ steel vessel.
H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)
If equilibrium mixture contains 1 mole of H₂, 1 mole of I₂ and 7 moles of HI. Calculate
(a) Equilibrium constant (Kc)
(b) Initial concentration of H₂ and I₂
questions.answer:
Given: volume of vessel V = 1 dm³; at equilibrium, n(H₂) = 1 mol, n(I₂) = 1 mol, n(HI) = 7 mol. Since V = 1 dm³, the equilibrium concentrations are [H₂] = 1 mol dm⁻³, [I₂] = 1 mol dm⁻³ and [HI] = 7 mol dm⁻³.
ICE table (amounts in mol; V = 1 dm³):
                     H₂(g)  +  I₂(g)  ⇌  2HI(g)
Initial:              a           a           0
Change:              −x          −x         +2x
Equilibrium:          1           1           7
From the HI column, 2x = 7, so x = 3.5 mol. From the H₂ column, a − x = 1, so a = 1 + 3.5 = 4.5 mol; the same value is obtained for I₂.
(a) Kc = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]) = (7)²/(1 × 1) = 49/1 = 49. Since Δn = 2 − 2 = 0, Kc has no units (the concentration units cancel).
(b) Initial concentrations: [H₂]₀ = 4.5 mol/1 dm³ = 4.5 mol dm⁻³ and [I₂]₀ = 4.5 mol/1 dm³ = 4.5 mol dm⁻³. That is 4.5 moles of each were originally taken in the vessel.
Printed answer: [Ans: Kc = 49, initial conc. of H₂ = I₂ = 4.5 moles].
questions.explanation: The ICE table links the equilibrium amounts to the initial amounts through the stoichiometry: 2 mol of HI are formed for every 1 mol of H₂ and 1 mol of I₂ consumed. The 7 mol of HI at equilibrium therefore required 3.5 mol of each reactant, so the initial amount of each reactant was 1 + 3.5 = 4.5 mol. Because the vessel volume is 1 dm³ the amounts in moles and the molar concentrations are numerically equal. Kc is the ratio [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]) with products in the numerator; Δn = 0, so Kc is dimensionless.

questions.question:
Lead fluoride (PbF₂) is a high melting white solid used in glass coating to reflect IR rays. Its solubility in water at 25°C is 0.58 g/dm³. Calculate its Ksp.
(At. mass of Pb = 207 and F = 19)
questions.answer:
Given: solubility of PbF₂ = 0.58 g dm⁻³; atomic masses Pb = 207, F = 19.
Molar mass of PbF₂ = 207 + 2 × 19 = 207 + 38 = 245 g mol⁻¹.
Molar solubility: s = (0.58 g dm⁻³)/(245 g mol⁻¹) = 2.367 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³.
Dissolution equilibrium: PbF₂(s) ⇌ Pb²⁺(aq) + 2F⁻(aq)
If s mol dm⁻³ of PbF₂ dissolves, then [Pb²⁺] = s = 2.367 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ and [F⁻] = 2s = 4.734 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³.
Ksp = [Pb²⁺][F⁻]² = s(2s)² = 4s³
Ksp = 4 × (2.367 × 10⁻³)³ = 4 × 1.327 × 10⁻⁸ = 5.31 × 10⁻⁸
The unit is (mol dm⁻³)³ = mol³ dm⁻⁹, because three ions are produced per formula unit.
Printed answer: [Ans: 5.3 × 10⁻⁸ mol³/dm⁹].
questions.explanation: The solubility is given in g dm⁻³, so it must first be converted to molar solubility by dividing by the molar mass of PbF₂ (245 g mol⁻¹). Each formula unit that dissolves gives one Pb²⁺ ion and two F⁻ ions, so [F⁻] is twice the molar solubility and the Ksp expression contains [F⁻]². Substituting gives Ksp = 4s³ = 5.3 × 10⁻⁸. A common error is to use s² instead of 4s³, which forgets that two fluoride ions are produced; the cube also fixes the units as mol³ dm⁻⁹.

questions.question: A solution of CaCO₃ is prepared by mixing 200 cm³ of 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ M Ca(NO₃)₂ and 300 cm³ of 4.5 × 10⁻² M K₂CO₃. Will CaCO₃ precipitate upon cooling to 25°C if Ksp of CaCO₃ at 25°C is 3.8 × 10⁻⁹.
questions.answer:
Given: V(Ca(NO₃)₂) = 200 cm³ = 0.200 dm³, M(Ca(NO₃)₂) = 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³; V(K₂CO₃) = 300 cm³ = 0.300 dm³, M(K₂CO₃) = 4.5 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³; Ksp(CaCO₃) = 3.8 × 10⁻⁹ at 25 °C.
Total volume after mixing = 200 + 300 = 500 cm³ = 0.500 dm³.
Moles of Ca²⁺ = 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.200 = 4.8 × 10⁻⁵ mol, so [Ca²⁺] = (4.8 × 10⁻⁵)/0.500 = 9.6 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³.
Moles of CO₃²⁻ = 4.5 × 10⁻² × 0.300 = 1.35 × 10⁻² mol, so [CO₃²⁻] = (1.35 × 10⁻²)/0.500 = 2.7 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³.
Ionic product Q = [Ca²⁺][CO₃²⁻] = (9.6 × 10⁻⁵)(2.7 × 10⁻²) = 2.59 × 10⁻⁶.
Comparison: Q = 2.59 × 10⁻⁶ and Ksp = 3.8 × 10⁻⁹, so Q > Ksp (about 680 times larger). The solution is supersaturated, therefore CaCO₃ will precipitate until the ionic product falls to Ksp.
Printed answer: [Ans: CaCO₃ precipitate].
questions.explanation: On mixing, both solutions are diluted by the total volume of 500 cm³, so each concentration must be multiplied by its own volume fraction (200/500 for Ca²⁺ and 300/500 for CO₃²⁻). The ionic product of the mixture is then compared with Ksp: Q < Ksp means no precipitate, Q = Ksp means a saturated solution, and Q > Ksp means precipitation. Here Q = 2.59 × 10⁻⁶ is far greater than 3.8 × 10⁻⁹, so calcium carbonate precipitates. The calculation also shows why the very dilute Ca(NO₃)₂ still gives a precipitate: the carbonate concentration is comparatively large.

questions.question:
Hydrogen iodide is a colourless gas prepared by reacting H₂ and I₂.
H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)
In an equilibrium study of above reaction, 1.2 mole of H₂ and 1.2 moles of I₂ were injected in an evacuated 1000 cm³ sealed flask and start the reaction to occur at 440°C until the equilibrium is formed. If Kc for this reaction is 49, calculate the equilibrium concentration of H₂, I₂ and HI.
questions.answer:
Given: V = 1000 cm³ = 1 dm³; initial n(H₂) = 1.2 mol, n(I₂) = 1.2 mol, n(HI) = 0; Kc = 49 at 440 °C. Therefore the initial concentrations are [H₂]₀ = [I₂]₀ = 1.2 mol dm⁻³ and [HI]₀ = 0.
Let x mol dm⁻³ of H₂ react to reach equilibrium.
ICE table (concentrations in mol dm⁻³):
                     H₂(g)  +  I₂(g)  ⇌  2HI(g)
Initial:              1.2         1.2          0
Change:               −x          −x         +2x
Equilibrium:        1.2 − x     1.2 − x       2x
Kc = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]) = (2x)²/(1.2 − x)² = 49
Taking the positive square root of both sides: 2x/(1.2 − x) = √49 = 7
2x = 7(1.2 − x) = 8.4 − 7x
2x + 7x = 8.4, so 9x = 8.4 and x = 0.933 mol dm⁻³.
Therefore [H₂] = 1.2 − 0.933 = 0.267 mol dm⁻³, [I₂] = 1.2 − 0.933 = 0.267 mol dm⁻³ and [HI] = 2 × 0.933 = 1.866 mol dm⁻³.
Check: (1.866)²/(0.267 × 0.267) = 3.48/0.0713 ≈ 48.9 ≈ 49, which agrees with the given Kc.
Printed answer: [Ans: [H₂] = 0.267 mol/dm³, [I₂] = 0.267 mol/dm³, [HI] = 1.866 mol/dm³].
questions.explanation: Because the flask volume is exactly 1 dm³, the initial amounts in moles are numerically equal to the initial molar concentrations. The ICE table uses the 1:1:2 stoichiometry: for every x mol dm⁻³ of H₂ consumed, x mol dm⁻³ of I₂ is also consumed and 2x mol dm⁻³ of HI is formed. The equilibrium expression then reduces to a perfect square, so taking the positive square root gives a simple linear equation; the negative root would give a physically meaningless negative concentration. The calculated values agree with the printed answer and satisfy Kc = 49.

questions.question: H₂SO₄ is stronger acid than CH₃COOH because:
questions.answer: (c) Its degree of ionization is high
questions.explanation: Acid strength is measured by the extent to which an acid donates protons to water, that is by its degree of ionization, not by the number of hydrogen atoms in its formula. H₂SO₄ is a strong acid: its first ionization is essentially complete, H₂SO₄ + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + HSO₄⁻, so a 0.1 M solution furnishes almost 0.1 M H₃O⁺. Acetic acid is a weak acid, CH₃COOH + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + CH₃COO⁻, with Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, so only about 1.3% of its molecules are ionized in 0.1 M solution. Option (a) confuses basicity (the number of replaceable hydrogen atoms) with acid strength: HCl, with only one hydrogen per molecule, is a much stronger acid than acetic acid. Boiling point (b) and corrosiveness (d) are physical properties and do not measure the tendency to release a proton. Hence (c), its degree of ionization is high.

options.text: It gives two H⁺ ion per molecule
Its degree of ionization is high

questions.optionsRaw: (a) It gives two H⁺ ion per molecule  (b) Its boiling point is high  (c) Its degree of ionization is high  (d) It is highly corrosive
questions.correctAnswer: (c) Its degree of ionization is high

questions.question: Al₂O₃ is amphoteric oxide because it reacts with:
questions.answer: (c) Both acids and base
questions.explanation: An amphoteric oxide is one that can neutralize both acids and bases, because it behaves as a base towards an acid and as an acid towards a base. Aluminium oxide dissolves in acids to give aluminium salts: Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O. It also dissolves in strong alkalis to give aluminates: Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O → 2Na[Al(OH)₄], or on fusion Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + H₂O. Since it reacts with both acids and bases it is amphoteric. An oxide that reacts only with acids is basic (Na₂O, CaO), and one that reacts only with bases is acidic (CO₂, SO₂). Hence (c), both acids and base.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Acids  (b) Base  (c) Both acids and base  (d) Neither acid nor base

questions.question: Which of the following is not a Buffer solution:
questions.answer: (d) NaOH/HCl
questions.explanation: A buffer is a mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base, or a weak base and its conjugate acid, in comparable amounts, so that it can absorb added H⁺ or OH⁻ with little change in pH. CH₃COOH/CH₃COONa is the standard acidic buffer (pH ≈ 4.7); Na₂CO₃/NaHCO₃ is a basic buffer built on the CO₃²⁻/HCO₃⁻ conjugate pair (pH ≈ 10.3); NH₄OH/NH₄Cl is a basic buffer built on the NH₃/NH₄⁺ pair (pH ≈ 9.25). NaOH/HCl, however, is a mixture of a strong acid and a strong base: they neutralize each other almost completely, H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, and neither a weak acid nor a weak base remains to absorb further additions, so the pH changes sharply. Such a mixture is not a buffer, hence (d).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) CH₃COOH/CH₃COONa  (b) Na₂CO₃/NaHCO₃  (c) NH₄OH/NH₄Cl  (d) NaOH/HCl

questions.question: Which oxide is amphoteric in nature:
questions.answer: (d) Al₂O₃
questions.explanation: K₂O and CaO are basic oxides: they are the anhydrides of the strong bases KOH and Ca(OH)₂ and react only with acids, for example K₂O + 2HCl → 2KCl + H₂O. CO₂ is an acidic oxide, the anhydride of carbonic acid; it dissolves in water to give H₂CO₃ and reacts with bases to give carbonates (CO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O) but does not react with acids. Al₂O₃ is amphoteric: it reacts with acids to give aluminium salts (Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O) and with alkalis to give aluminates (Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O → 2Na[Al(OH)₄]). Hence the amphoteric oxide is Al₂O₃, option (d).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) K₂O  (b) CO₂  (c) CaO  (d) Al₂O₃

questions.question: Which of the following does not alter the pH of a solution?
questions.answer: (c) NaCl
questions.explanation: A salt changes the pH of water only if one of its ions hydrolyses. NaCl is the salt of a strong acid (HCl) and a strong base (NaOH): Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid and Na⁺ is the conjugate acid of a strong base, so neither ion reacts with water to any measurable extent and a NaCl solution stays neutral at pH 7. NH₄Cl is acidic because NH₄⁺ hydrolyses (NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺), Na₂CO₃ is alkaline because CO₃²⁻ hydrolyses (CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻), while Mg(OH)Cl is a basic salt whose solution is alkaline because it contains OH⁻ in addition to Cl⁻. Hence NaCl, option (c), does not alter the pH.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) NH₄Cl  (b) Na₂CO₃  (c) NaCl  (d) Mg(OH)Cl

questions.question: Conjugated acid of NH₃ is:
questions.answer: (a) NH₄⁺
questions.explanation: In the Brønsted-Lowry theory an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor, and a conjugate acid is the species formed when a base accepts one proton. Ammonia accepts a proton from water, NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻, so NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of NH₃ and NH₃ is the conjugate base of NH₄⁺; the two differ by exactly one proton. NH₂⁻ is obtained by removing H⁺ from NH₃ and is therefore the conjugate base formed when ammonia itself acts as an acid (NH₃ ⇌ NH₂⁻ + H⁺), not its conjugate acid. NH₂ and NH are not related to ammonia by the gain of a proton. Hence (a), NH₄⁺.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) NH₄⁺  (b) NH₂⁻  (c) NH₂  (d) NH

questions.question: Salt which is formed by the neutralization of weak acid and strong base is:
questions.answer: (c) Na₂CO₃
questions.explanation: The nature of a salt is fixed by the strengths of the acid and the base from which it is formed. Na₂CO₃ is obtained when carbonic acid, a weak acid, is neutralized by sodium hydroxide, a strong base: H₂CO₃ + 2NaOH → Na₂CO₃ + 2H₂O. Its anion hydrolyses, CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻, so the solution is alkaline. NaNO₃ is formed from HNO₃ (strong acid) and NaOH (strong base); NH₄Cl from HCl (strong acid) and NH₄OH (weak base); NH₄CN from HCN (weak acid) and NH₄OH (weak base). The salt of a weak acid and a strong base is therefore Na₂CO₃, option (c).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) NaNO₃  (b) NH₄Cl  (c) Na₂CO₃  (d) NH₄CN

questions.question: Which of the following statements is not correct about the bases?
questions.answer: (d) They turn blue litmus red
questions.explanation: Bases have a bitter taste (a) and a soapy feel, they give pH values above 7 (b), and they neutralize acids to form a salt and water (c), for example NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O. Their action on indicators is the opposite of that of acids: bases turn red litmus blue and leave blue litmus blue, whereas it is acids that turn blue litmus red. Statement (d) therefore describes an acid and not a base, so it is the incorrect statement about bases that the question asks for.

options.text: They react with acids to form salts

questions.optionsRaw: (a) They have bitter tastes  (b) They have high pH value  (c) They react with acids to form salts  (d) They turn blue litmus red

questions.question: A conjugate acid base pair has the difference of only:
questions.answer: (b) One proton
questions.explanation: According to Brønsted and Lowry an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor, and a conjugate acid-base pair consists of two species that differ by exactly one proton. For example CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻ differ by one H⁺, NH₄⁺ and NH₃ differ by one H⁺, and H₃O⁺ and H₂O differ by one H⁺. A proton is the hydrogen ion H⁺, so the difference is one proton, not one electron or one electron pair. The electron-pair relationship belongs to the Lewis theory, in which an acid accepts and a base donates a pair of electrons. Hence (b), one proton.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) One electron  (b) One proton  (c) One electron pair  (d) One proton pair

questions.question: Salt formed by neutralization of weak acid and weak base is:
questions.answer: (c) NH₄CN
questions.explanation: NH₄CN is obtained by neutralizing hydrocyanic acid, HCN, a weak acid, with ammonium hydroxide, NH₄OH, a weak base: HCN + NH₄OH → NH₄CN + H₂O. In solution both ions hydrolyse: NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺ and CN⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCN + OH⁻. Since Ka(HCN) = 4.9 × 10⁻¹⁰ is smaller than Kb(NH₃) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, the basic hydrolysis predominates and the solution is slightly alkaline (pH ≈ 9.3). NH₄Cl is a strong acid-weak base salt, Na₂CO₃ a weak acid-strong base salt and Na₂SO₄ a strong acid-strong base salt, so none of them is made from a weak acid and a weak base. Hence (c).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) NH₄Cl  (b) Na₂CO₃  (c) NH₄CN  (d) Na₂SO₄

questions.question: Define pH & pOH of a solution? Also show that pH + pOH = 14.
questions.answer:
pH: The pH of a solution is the negative logarithm to the base 10 of its hydrogen ion (hydronium ion) concentration expressed in moles per cubic decimetre: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], or pH = −log₁₀[H₃O⁺]. It measures the acidity of a solution on a scale that usually runs from 0 to 14 at 25 °C: pH < 7 for an acidic solution, pH = 7 for a neutral solution and pH > 7 for a basic solution. Because the scale is logarithmic, a change of one pH unit means a tenfold change in [H⁺]; for example [H⁺] = 10⁻³ M gives pH = 3.
pOH: pOH is the negative logarithm of the hydroxide ion concentration: pOH = −log₁₀[OH⁻]. It measures the basicity of a solution, so a high pOH corresponds to a low [OH⁻] and an acidic solution.
